    # Codex integration
    
    ## Install and locate the plugin
    
    For the desktop app, install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357). This listing is desktop-only.
    
    For Codex CLI, install the whole plugin, including its personas and standards:
    
    ```sh
    codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
    codex plugin add egm@egm
    ```
    
    Start a fresh session after installation. Select the installed `egm` skill
    from the available skills. Use its discovered absolute `SKILL.md` path;
    do not assume a particular cache directory, version, or checkout location.
    
    From `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`, the plugin root is three parent
    directories above the file. Resolve bundled `agents/`, `resources/`, and
    `docs/` paths against that root. Resolve `references/` against the active
    skill's directory. Resolve user documents and generated artifacts against
    the user's working directory. Never substitute similarly named files in the
    user's project for bundled personas or standards.
    
    If the user's prompt or agent instructions file (`AGENTS.md`) has a line
    `EGM artifact directory: <path>`, write briefs, drafts, and reports to that
    folder. Resolve a relative path against the working directory. If a path from
    `AGENTS.md` resolves outside the working directory, after following symbolic
    links, ask the user to confirm it before creating the folder or writing there.
    If they decline or no one can confirm, use the working directory and say why.
    Create the folder if it does not exist.
    
    In ChatGPT Work, a skill may be exposed through a cloud resource identifier
    while supporting files live in the installed local bundle. Use the installed
    path supplied by the skill inventory or installation metadata for those files;
    do not construct cloud resource identifiers for arbitrary supporting paths.
    If no installed path is available, report the missing capability instead of
    guessing a cache location. Read reviewer filenames and frontmatter from the
    bundle: a role such as `egm-design` maps to `agents/design_critic.md`, not
    `agents/design.md`. Confirm each resolved path before dispatch.
    
    ## Fresh-context reviewers
    
    Inspect the available native subagent tool schema. Tool names can be
    namespaced and vary by Codex version. When `spawn_agent` exposes
    `fork_context`, explicitly set `fork_context: false` for every Goldfish.
    When the schema instead exposes `fork_turns`, use `fork_turns: "none"`.
    This applies to reviewers launched by a synthesizer too. Use a general-purpose agent
    and pass absolute paths to the persona, standards, target document, and
    explicitly selected reading list. Do not pass the parent transcript, private
    reasoning, or answers the document is supposed to explain.
    
    Require the reviewer to read its persona, target, and every supplied standard
    before returning findings. A missing read or inaccessible file is an incomplete
    review, not a clean result. Verify native tool results when the host exposes
    them; a parent-written completion summary is not equivalent evidence.
    
    Wait for actual reviewer completion before synthesizing findings. Propagate
    failures and timeouts; a launched reviewer is not a completed review. If
    nesting is unavailable, dispatch reviewers directly from the parent while
    preserving the same isolation. If the available tool cannot establish a fresh
    context, stop the Goldfish review and report that limitation.
    
    Fresh conversation context does not isolate the filesystem, configured memory
    services, or project instructions. Do not retrieve conversation history or
    memory to supply missing design context. An isolation test should use a unique
    parent-only marker and check the actual child result, not the parent's claim.
    
    The `fork_context: false` and `fork_turns: "none"` options concern parent
    conversation turns. They do not prove that Codex excludes host instruction
    files. Issue [#237](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/237)
    reports that Codex CLI 0.166.0 injected project and user `AGENTS.md` files
    despite `fork_turns: "none"`. Treat instruction-file exclusion as unverified
    unless a separate child-context probe confirms it for the tested host version.
    
    ## Questions and artifacts
    
    The shared skills' question payloads describe the intended interaction, not a
    literal Codex API. Use a structured question tool only when it is available
    and permitted in the current mode, mapping to its actual schema. Otherwise
    ask one plain-text question and wait for the answer. Preserve the skill's

    # Z framework engineering principles
    
    Part of the repository guidance mapped in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).
    Read before code changes; consult the map for task-specific rules.
    
    **Act as a principal software engineer who is a leading global expert
    in performance-oriented low-latency C++ systems and network programming.**
    
    ## Target systems
    - compilers: current gcc, clang
    - CPU: x64 intel/amd, ARM
    - OS: linux, windows
    
    ## General principles
    - time-to-market / engineering velocity is less important than:
      - design/implementation integrity
      - run-time performance
    - latency is more important than throughput
    - copying and heap memory allocations are minimized
      - where heap allocations are necessary, they use tunable heaps, except for
        objects managed by `ZmSingleton` or `ZmSpecific`
    - dependent compatibility is a non-goal unless otherwise directed
      - propagate breaking API changes to dependent code
      - do not use shims, forwarders or other such techniques for legacy compatibility purposes
    - software must be capable of running 24x7 indefinitely without process kill
      - prohibit monotonically growing memory consumption
      - all long-lived containers must be actively garbage collected
    - shutdown/teardown must be graceful and clean of leaks
    - no background garbage collection or scanning for GC
      - garbage collection must be deterministic, timely and not timer-based
    - intrusive reference counting and container nodes
    - sharding:
      - controlled thread creation
      - threads dedicated to specific work and thread-affined data
      - fast inter-thread communication with ring buffers
    - asynchronous continuation-based functional style
    
    ### No dogma
    - immutability
      - pervasive immutability is a non-goal
      - mutability is encouraged if it benefits performance
        - example: in-place encrypt plaintext, decrypt ciphertext for TLS
        - example: in-place decoding of strings in JSON parsing
    - type punning and undefined behavior
      - avoiding UB that is purely theoretical or limited to non-targeted systems is a non-goal
      - UB type punning is endorsed unless it actually creates a **tangible correctness or security risk** for targeted systems
    - not header-only
      - **intentionally** not header-only
      - Z libraries are traditional hybrid builds
        - headers with accompanying binary versioned shared libraries / DLLs
    - intrusive + intrinsic
      - non-intrusive or extrinsic storage is a non-goal (no STL containers)
    - sentinel values
      - sentinel values for logical null or false, not extrinsic booleans
    - Postel's Law, unabashedly
      - “Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept.”
      - conformance policing is a non-goal
      - elide all excessive correctness and validation in favor of performance
      - this principle applied to all protocols and formats for maximum resilience
    # Zxdp implementation rules
    
    Follow the repository guidance in ../AGENTS.md and the caller-supplied
    [interface contract](INTERFACE.md). The contract supersedes earlier plans.
    
    * Creation takes named parameters: interface, optional destination network mask,
      intrusive Tx pool list with count and size, one dedicated Rx pool, receive
      callback. No transmit-completion callback. Without a mask all traffic is selected.
    * Keep allocation and kernel leases distinct in preallocated slot bookkeeping.
      Explicit pool return may run before or after CQ. Recycle only after both leases
      end; safe close releases kernel leases while caller-held backing stays valid.
      One descriptor may be outstanding for a slot. Rejected send acquires no lease.
    * Application and transport adaptation belongs to the caller. This library owns
      arena provisioning, raw packet allocation/return and kernel ring service.
    * Preallocate arenas and all packet bookkeeping at setup. Recycle each pool with
      the non-sharded ZmHeap payload-overlay slist. Exhaustion returns null.
    * Packet lookup and completion use direct slot identity, with constant-time
      updates. No packet/buffer searches or hot-path heap allocations.
    * Query kernel ring mapping offsets and preserve SWSR ownership. The caller
      provides one Rx service owner and one Tx service owner; final pool return may
      run on any thread. Keep thread-exclusive mutable state on separate cache lines.
    * Construct payload directly in registered backing. No payload staging or copy.
    * Quiesce service before close. Retire kernel access before returning submitted
      backing. A caller-owned pool retains its arena through the last packet return.
    * Queue configuration and mask compilation are cold-path operations.
    * Own the required `rx()`/`wake()` pair: spin for a configurable count before
      blocking with the most efficient suitable kernel mechanism; receive packets
      until explicitly woken, then return. With epoll, post wakeups through an
      internal `eventfd`, following ZiEventLoop/ZiMultiplex, with no per-wakeup
      allocation. Own these descriptors and their lifecycle. Wake
      must interrupt spinning and blocking promptly, including under continuous
      traffic and at the transition into the wait. Internal batches do not cause
      `rx()` to return on their own. The caller owns scheduling and lifecycle retries.

    //  -*- mode:c++; indent-tabs-mode:t; tab-width:8; c-basic-offset:2; -*-
    //  vi: noet ts=8 sw=2 cino=+0,(s,l1,m1,g0,N-s,j1,U1,W2,i2
    
    // (c) Copyright 2026 Huw Rogers
    // This code is licensed by the MIT license (see LICENSE for details)
    
    // Raw AF_XDP arena, pool and packet facilities.
    
    #ifndef Zxdp_HH
    #define Zxdp_HH
    
    #ifndef ZxdpLib_HH
    #include <zlib/ZxdpLib.hh>
    #endif
    
    #include <stdint.h>
    #include <zlib/ZuSpan.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZuUnion.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZmFn.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZmRef.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZmPolymorph.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZtString.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZePlatform.hh>
    #include <zlib/ZxdpAlloc.hh>
    
    namespace Zxdp {
    
    using RecvFn = ZmFn<void(uint8_t *, unsigned), ZmFnHeapID<"Zxdp.Receive">>;
    // Canonical backing and retired submission count. Keep repeated submissions
    // immutable until all completions; close may coalesce their remaining counts.
    using CompleteFn = ZmFn<void(uint8_t *, unsigned), ZmFnHeapID<"Zxdp.Complete">>;
    
    struct Params {
      unsigned interface = 0; // network-interface index in the current namespace
      ZuCSpan netmask;       // optional destination CIDR; empty takes all traffic
      BufPool *txPools = nullptr;
      BufPool *rxPool = nullptr;
      RecvFn rx;
      CompleteFn txCompleted;
      unsigned spin = 1000; // empty receive probe rounds before blocking in epoll
    };
    
    // The caller drives Rx/Tx on their respective single owners. Allocation/free
    // may run on other threads. Backing stays owned by the caller through completion.
    class ZxdpAPI Instance : public ZmPolymorph {
    friend struct InstanceData;
    
    public:
      // Normally null on failure. A non-ready handle with an error retains any
      // pending kernel rollback; keep it and retry close until it completes.
      static ZmRef<Instance> create(Params, ZtString<> &error);
      ~Instance() override;
      Instance(const Instance &) = delete;
      Instance &operator =(const Instance &) = delete;
    
      bool ready() const;
      unsigned ifindex() const;
      unsigned mtu() const;
      bool zeroCopy() const;
      ZuBSpan mac() const;
    
      bool send(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length);
      // Process packets on the Rx owner until woken (or the device fails).
      // Idle service spins Params::spin rounds, then blocks internally in epoll.
      void rx();
      // Any thread, including the receive callback. Each posted wake returns one
      // rx() call; a wake before entry remains pending. No per-wake allocation.
      void wake();
      unsigned pollTx();
    
      // Wake/join Rx and quiesce Tx and all wake callers first. An exception result
      // preserves the handle for retry; only successful kernel retirement permits
      // pending backing to return.
      // Void means success; an empty exception means retirement is pending.
      ZuUnion<void, ZeException> close();
    
    private:
      explicit Instance(InstanceData *data) : m_data{data} { }
      InstanceData *m_data;
    };
    
    } // namespace Zxdp
    #endif /* Zxdp_HH */

    ## Assistant
    
    Yes—use a **software poll-mode driver (PMD)**. No physical NIC, VFIO binding, or IOMMU is needed.
    
    **For a simple TX → RX loopback, use `net_ring`.** It exposes an in-memory ring through the normal DPDK Ethernet APIs. DPDK documents this specifically for testing without Ethernet hardware. [Ring PMD documentation](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/ring.html)
    
    Assuming `dpdk-testpmd` and the ring driver are installed:
    
    ```bash
    # Replace 0-1 with two CPUs available to your process.
    dpdk-testpmd -l 0-1 \
      --no-pci --no-huge --no-shconf -m 256 \
      --vdev=net_ring0 \
      -- -i --nb-cores=1 --total-num-mbufs=4096 \
      --rxq=1 --txq=1 --disable-rss \
      --port-topology=loop --forward-mode=io
    ```
    
    At its prompt:
    
    ```text
    start tx_first
    show port stats all
    stop
    quit
    ```
    
    Wait a few seconds before displaying statistics. `start tx_first` injects the initial packets; forwarding then circulates them through the ring. RX and TX counters should increase. Plain `start` has no initial traffic to circulate. [Testpmd commands](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/testpmd_app_ug/testpmd_funcs.html)
    
    Here, `--no-pci` disables PCI discovery and `--no-huge` uses ordinary memory, avoiding hugepage setup. This configuration does not support DPDK primary/secondary shared-memory operation. [EAL options](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/linux_gsg/linux_eal_parameters.html)
    
    **For testing your actual TCP/UDP application, choose the connection you need:**
    
    | Test arrangement | Suitable approach |
    |---|---|
    | One process, packet loopback | `net_ring` |
    | Two endpoints within one process | Two ports created with `rte_eth_from_rings()`, with RX/TX rings cross-connected |
    | Linux socket client ↔ DPDK protocol stack | `net_tap` |
    | Two independent DPDK processes | Linux `veth` pair, with `net_af_packet` attached to each end |
    | Repeatable packet input/output | `net_pcap` with input/output capture files |
    
    These are supported by the [ring](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/ring.html), [TAP](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/tap.html), [AF_PACKET](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/af_packet.html), and [PCAP](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides-24.11/nics/pcap_ring.html) drivers.
    
    For example, launch your protocol-stack application with these **EAL arguments**:
    
    ```bash
    sudo ./your-app -l 0-1 --no-pci --no-huge \
      --vdev=net_tap0,iface=dtap0 -- <application-options>
    ```
    
    Then configure the Linux side:
    
    ```bash
    sudo ip addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev dtap0
    sudo ip link set dtap0 up
    ```
    
    Configure **192.0.2.2/24 inside your DPDK application’s stack**, and connect from Linux to that address. Do not assign `.2` to Linux as well: local routing would bypass your application. The application must implement the relevant ARP/IP/TCP/UDP handling; DPDK itself supplies packet I/O.
    
    Use these setups for functional testing and software-path measurements. They do not validate physical NIC DMA, hardware offloads, or wire latency.

    $ cat zxdp/README.md; rg -n 'Instance|Params|rx\(|tx\(|alloc|free|init|final' zxdp/src/Zxdp.cc; rg --files zxdp; rg -n '^#' docs/CPP.md docs/IO.md docs/BUILD.md
    # Zxdp: Linux AF_XDP packet I/O
    
    Zxdp supplies raw AF_XDP packet arenas, intrusive pools and kernel ring service.
    The [interface contract](INTERFACE.md) defines its boundary. The caller supplies
    transport state, application adaptation and scheduling.
    Include `<zlib/Zxdp.hh>` and link `libZxdp` and its framework dependencies.
    For Zi provider and transport integration see [Zutcp](../zutcp/README.md).
    Both modules are Linux-only and are excluded from Windows builds.
    
    ## Interface
    
    Include `Zxdp.hh`. Create an `Instance` with named `Params` members:
    
    * `interface`: network-interface index in the current network namespace.
    * `netmask`: optional destination IPv4/IPv6 CIDR. An empty mask selects all
      interface traffic, including non-IP frames. Unmatched traffic passes to the
      kernel. The classifier handles Ethernet and up to two VLAN tags.
    * `txPools`: head of the caller-owned intrusive `BufPool::next` list. Each pool
      supplies `count` and maximum packet `size`.
    * `rxPool`: one nonempty caller-owned pool with a dedicated Rx region.
    * `rx`: callback receiving the raw packet address and length.
    * `spin`: idle probe rounds before the receive loop blocks (default 1000).
    
    Allocate with `txPool.alloc()`, construct the complete Ethernet packet directly
    in that backing and call `instance->send(packet, length)`. A false return leaves
    ownership with the caller. A true return publishes a descriptor and holds a kernel
    lease; keep bytes immutable until kernel retirement. Explicitly return the caller's
    allocation lease with `pool.free(packet)`. Recycling waits for both leases to end,
    so return may precede CQ. Kernel completion does not prove successful wire delivery.
    Exhaustion returns null and never allocates a replacement.
    Rx callbacks likewise own their packet until they return it to the Rx pool.
    An advanced Rx wire pointer can be passed directly to `rxPool.free()`.
    
    One descriptor may be outstanding for a slot. A caller can retain its allocation
    lease past CQ and resubmit the same backing, then return it when transport recovery
    permits. `pollTx()` returns the number of kernel submissions retired and releases
    their kernel leases; there is no completion callback or application packet object.
    
    ## Arenas and service
    
    Setup reserves one contiguous registered UMEM mapping containing disjoint,
    page-aligned Rx and Tx arena regions. Rx has one pool; Tx pools partition its
    region according to each count and size, rounded for alignment. The recycling
    slist overlays free payload exactly as in non-sharded ZmHeap arenas. Pools retain
    the mapping through their last packet return. Packet bookkeeping, direct page
    ownership lookup and active slot arrays are allocated during setup.
    
    `rx()` runs on the caller's Rx owner. It processes packets and invokes the
    receive callback until explicitly woken. On idle input it probes the mapped
    rings for `Params::spin` rounds (default 1000), then blocks in epoll on packet
    readiness and an internal eventfd. A round probes the configured Rx queues;
    zero spin goes directly to the wait after checking available work. Packet
    arrival resumes processing inside the same call, rather than returning it.
    
    `wake()` may run on any thread, including the receive callback. It posts to the
    internal eventfd and interrupts spinning, blocking or active processing so
    `rx()` returns. Each posted wake permits one return, including wakes before
    entry; concurrent posts are preserved. Kernel wait descriptors remain private.
    `pollTx()` services bounded completion turns on the caller's Tx owner.
    
    Allocation and return can run on other threads. Every interface Rx queue is bound
    to the shared registration and has a reserved share of the Rx pool. Tx uses queue
    zero. After an off-owner return to a depleted pool, wake the receive owner and
    arrange another `rx()` entry to replenish input. All packet service and wake
    operations use preallocated state; they perform no heap allocation or packet/
    buffer searches. Wake/join the receiver and quiesce Tx and wake callers before
    close.
    
    Creation and close are control-path operations. Quiesce both service owners before
    calling `close()`. Its `ZuUnion<void, ZeException>` result holds `void` on success;
    an empty exception means retry is pending. A populated exception
    retains the handle for explicit recovery/retry. Submitted backing is returned only
    after kernel queue retirement has been observed. Continue close until successful,
    then release the instance. Caller-owned pools outlive the instance and all
    outstanding raw packets. Freeze their configuration while bound.
    
    Creation normally returns null on failure. If kernel rollback is still pending,
    it returns a non-ready handle with an error; retain that handle and finish close.
    The interface must have no unrelated XDP attachment. Guarded attach/detach protects
    other owners, including changes concurrent with control operations.
    
    ## Verification
    
    Build the configured tree with `make -j8`; run `make -C zxdp/test test` for
    unprivileged tests. See [integration tests](itest/README.md) for scoped privileged
    kernel tests and [utilities](util/README.md) for independent packet processes.
    The implementation targets Linux AF_XDP with single-frame packets fitting one
    kernel chunk. Physical NIC zero-copy requires driver support and separate hardware
    validation; veth verifies software-copy operation only.

    namespace Zxdp {
    
    class UMem;
    class BufPool;
    struct InstanceData;
    
    struct PoolParams {
      BufPool *next = nullptr;
      unsigned count = 0;
      unsigned size = 0;
    };
    
    // Keep pool objects alive through instance close and final packet return.
    // Freeze the list/count/size while bound. Exhaustion never allocates backing.
    class ZxdpAPI BufPool : public ZmNHeap<BufPool>, public PoolParams {
    friend inline ZuStringT<"Zxdp.Pool"> ZmNHeapID(BufPool *);
    friend class UMem;
    friend struct InstanceData;
    
    public:
      enum { NoSlot = unsigned(-1) };
      BufPool(unsigned count = 0, unsigned size = 0);
      ~BufPool();
      BufPool(const BufPool &) = delete;
      BufPool &operator =(const BufPool &) = delete;
    
      uint8_t *alloc();
      void free(void *packet);
      unsigned used() const { return unsigned(m_used); }
      bool ready() const { return unsigned(m_active); }
      bool owns(const void *) const;
      unsigned slot(const void *) const;
      uint8_t *backing(unsigned slot) const;
    
    private:
      void init(ZmRef<UMem>, uint64_t offset, unsigned stride, unsigned prefix, unsigned first);
      void retire() { m_active = 0; }
      UMem *arena() const { return m_arena; }
      unsigned first() const { return m_first; }
      unsigned stride() const { return unsigned(1)<<m_shift; }
      uint64_t offset() const { return m_offset; }
    
      using Head = ZmAtomic<uintptr_t>;
      using Count = ZmAtomic<unsigned>;
      ZmRef<UMem>    m_arena;
      uint64_t    m_offset = 0;
      unsigned    m_shift = 0, m_prefix = 0, m_first = 0;
      alignas(Zm::CacheLineSize) Head m_head{0};
      Count        m_used{0}, m_active{0};
    };
    
    } // namespace Zxdp
    #endif /* ZxdpAlloc_HH */

    ## Assistant
    
    Yes—use a **software poll-mode driver (PMD)**. No physical NIC, VFIO binding, or IOMMU is needed.
    
    **For a simple TX → RX loopback, use `net_ring`.** It exposes an in-memory ring through the normal DPDK Ethernet APIs. DPDK documents this specifically for testing without Ethernet hardware. [Ring PMD documentation](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/ring.html)
    
    Assuming `dpdk-testpmd` and the ring driver are installed:
    
    ```bash
    # Replace 0-1 with two CPUs available to your process.
    dpdk-testpmd -l 0-1 \
      --no-pci --no-huge --no-shconf -m 256 \
      --vdev=net_ring0 \
      -- -i --nb-cores=1 --total-num-mbufs=4096 \
      --rxq=1 --txq=1 --disable-rss \
      --port-topology=loop --forward-mode=io
    ```
    
    At its prompt:
    
    ```text
    start tx_first
    show port stats all
    stop
    quit
    ```
    
    Wait a few seconds before displaying statistics. `start tx_first` injects the initial packets; forwarding then circulates them through the ring. RX and TX counters should increase. Plain `start` has no initial traffic to circulate. [Testpmd commands](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/testpmd_app_ug/testpmd_funcs.html)
    
    Here, `--no-pci` disables PCI discovery and `--no-huge` uses ordinary memory, avoiding hugepage setup. This configuration does not support DPDK primary/secondary shared-memory operation. [EAL options](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/linux_gsg/linux_eal_parameters.html)
    
    **For testing your actual TCP/UDP application, choose the connection you need:**
    
    | Test arrangement | Suitable approach |
    |---|---|
    | One process, packet loopback | `net_ring` |
    | Two endpoints within one process | Two ports created with `rte_eth_from_rings()`, with RX/TX rings cross-connected |
    | Linux socket client ↔ DPDK protocol stack | `net_tap` |
    | Two independent DPDK processes | Linux `veth` pair, with `net_af_packet` attached to each end |
    | Repeatable packet input/output | `net_pcap` with input/output capture files |
    
    These are supported by the [ring](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/ring.html), [TAP](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/tap.html), [AF_PACKET](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/af_packet.html), and [PCAP](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides-24.11/nics/pcap_ring.html) drivers.
    
    For example, launch your protocol-stack application with these **EAL arguments**:
    
    ```bash
    sudo ./your-app -l 0-1 --no-pci --no-huge \
      --vdev=net_tap0,iface=dtap0 -- <application-options>
    ```
    
    Then configure the Linux side:
    
    ```bash
    sudo ip addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev dtap0
    sudo ip link set dtap0 up
    ```
    
    Configure **192.0.2.2/24 inside your DPDK application’s stack**, and connect from Linux to that address. Do not assign `.2` to Linux as well: local routing would bypass your application. The application must implement the relevant ARP/IP/TCP/UDP handling; DPDK itself supplies packet I/O.
    
    Use these setups for functional testing and software-path measurements. They do not validate physical NIC DMA, hardware offloads, or wire latency.

    # Backend boundary
    
    This is the implementation contract supplied by the caller. It supersedes the
    earlier expanded interface in this module.
    
    Instance creation takes named parameters:
    
    * Network interface.
    * Optional network mask for packet selection. Without a mask, XDP takes over
      all traffic on the interface.
    * Head of an intrusive list of Tx pools. Each pool supplies count and packet
      size. Provision the Tx arena from that list and initialize one recycling
      free list per pool.
    * One Rx pool, with its own dedicated Rx arena.
    * Raw packet receive callback.
    
    There is no transmit-completion callback. Allocation holds one caller lease;
    accepted submission holds a separate kernel lease. Explicit pool return releases
    the caller lease, and kernel CQ or safe close releases the kernel lease. Recycle
    only when both are gone. Return may precede CQ; a caller can also retain backing
    past CQ for retransmission and return it later. Rejected send adds no kernel lease.
    One descriptor may be outstanding for an allocated slot at a time.
    
    The packet operations are allocation from a Tx pool, return to an Rx or Tx pool,
    and submission of a Tx packet. Application and transport object ownership is
    outside this module. The caller owns adapter composition.
    
    All arenas, ring mappings and packet bookkeeping are allocated during setup.
    Packet service performs no heap allocation. Allocation and return use the
    agreed non-sharded ZmHeap payload-overlay slist. Packet admission, receive and
    completion resolve backing directly; they never search packets or buffers.
    
    The receive entry is `rx()`: process incoming packets through the configured
    callback, spin for a configurable count when idle, then use the most efficient
    suitable kernel blocking mechanism. An epoll implementation waits on packet
    readiness and an internal `eventfd`, following ZiEventLoop/ZiMultiplex. Packet
    readiness resumes processing; the call returns when explicitly woken. Expose
    `wake()` for Zutcp to interrupt the spinning or blocked receive loop and cause
    `rx()` to return. With epoll, `wake()` posts to that `eventfd`; no per-wakeup
    object is allocated. Wake observation must remain prompt during continuous traffic
    and must not be lost at the transition into epoll. The wait mechanism and its
    internal descriptors belong to this library; caller scheduling remains outside.
    
    Zutcp delegates its plugin `rx()`/`wake()` hooks to this pair. Internal driver
    NEED_WAKEUP handling and safe kernel retirement also remain in this library.
    These facilities must not grow into a second transport or application runtime.
    The public receive/wake pair owns the eventfd/epoll mechanism; raw readiness
    descriptors and a nonblocking receive-poll entry are not exposed.
    
    Current receive/wake validation covers preposted and concurrent pulses, wake
    races at epoll entry, continued receive processing after packet readiness, and
    wake during active callbacks. Full transport integration and hardware DMA
    validation remain separate work.

    # Zxdp implementation rules
    
    Follow the repository guidance in ../AGENTS.md and the caller-supplied
    [interface contract](INTERFACE.md). The contract supersedes earlier plans.
    
    * Creation takes named parameters: interface, optional destination network mask,
      intrusive Tx pool list with count and size, one dedicated Rx pool, receive
      callback. No transmit-completion callback. Without a mask all traffic is selected.
    * Keep allocation and kernel leases distinct in preallocated slot bookkeeping.
      Explicit pool return may run before or after CQ. Recycle only after both leases
      end; safe close releases kernel leases while caller-held backing stays valid.
      One descriptor may be outstanding for a slot. Rejected send acquires no lease.
      The Tx-owner writable query requires a caller-held allocation and reads only
      existing direct-slot lease state. It authorizes header changes after kernel
      retirement, with no new callback, tracking allocation or packet search.
    * The optional borrowed send commit hook runs synchronously after successful
      ring reservation, before slot/lease mutation and descriptor publication. False
      cancels the reservation; true permits no later refusal. It is not a completion
      callback and must not retain context, throw, reenter Tx service or queue work.
      Use raw-context `ZmFn` binding without callback allocation on the packet path.
    * Application and transport adaptation belongs to the caller. This library owns
      arena provisioning, raw packet allocation/return and kernel ring service.
    * Preallocate arenas and all packet bookkeeping at setup. Recycle each pool with
      the non-sharded ZmHeap payload-overlay slist. Exhaustion returns null.
    * Packet lookup and completion use direct slot identity, with constant-time
      updates. No packet/buffer searches or hot-path heap allocations.
    * Query kernel ring mapping offsets and preserve SWSR ownership. The caller

    namespace Zxdp {
    
    using CommitFn = ZmFn<bool()>;
    
    using RecvFn = ZmFn<void(uint8_t *, unsigned), ZmFnHeapID<"Zxdp.Receive">>;
    using StopFn = ZmFn<void(), ZmFnHeapID<"Zxdp.TxStopped">>;
    
    struct Params {
      unsigned interface = 0; // network-interface index in the current namespace
      ZuCSpan netmask;       // optional destination CIDR; empty takes all traffic
      BufPool *txPools = nullptr;
      BufPool *rxPool = nullptr;
      RecvFn rx;
      unsigned spin = 1000; // idle probes before Rx blocks or Tx service returns
      ZmScheduler *scheduler = nullptr; // caller-owned scheduler
      unsigned txSid = 0; // application-assigned sender slot
      ZmSchedTParams txThread = ZmSchedTParams().isolated(true); // apply to slot before start
      StopFn txStopped; // optional owner continuation after sender callbacks drain
    };
    
    // The caller drives Rx/Tx on their respective single owners. Allocation/free
    // may run on other threads. Allocation holds backing until explicit pool return;
    // an accepted send also holds it until kernel completion or safe close.
    class ZxdpAPI Instance : public ZmPolymorph {
    friend struct InstanceData;
    
    public:
      // Normally null on failure. A non-ready handle with an error retains any
      // pending kernel rollback; keep it and retry close until it completes.
      static ZmRef<Instance> create(Params, ZtString<> &error);
      ~Instance() override;
      Instance(const Instance &) = delete;
      Instance &operator =(const Instance &) = delete;
    
      bool ready() const;
      unsigned ifindex() const;
      unsigned mtu() const;
      bool zeroCopy() const;
      ZuBSpan mac() const;
      // False acquires no kernel lease. After true, keep bytes immutable until
      // kernel retirement. Pool return may precede retirement; recycling waits for
      // both the allocation lease and kernel lease to end. One descriptor per slot.
      // Borrowed synchronous commit hook: false cancels admission without a lease;
      // true promises immediate descriptor publication with no further refusal.
      bool send(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length, const CommitFn &commit = {});
      // Process packets on the Rx owner until woken (or the device fails).
      // Idle service spins Params::spin rounds, then blocks internally in epoll.
      void rx();
      // Any thread, including the receive callback. Each posted wake returns one
      // rx() call; a wake before entry remains pending. No per-wake allocation.
      void wake();
      unsigned pollTx(); // number of kernel submissions retired this turn
      // Synchronous enumeration; consume telemetry inside the callback. Closed
      // instances retain final ring views until destruction, without live mappings.
      unsigned allQueues(Ztc::QueueMgr::AllFn) const;
      bool stopSender(); // quiesce sender slot; completion arrives through txStopped
    
      // Wake/join Rx and quiesce Tx and all wake callers first. An exception result
      // preserves the handle for retry; only successful kernel retirement permits
      // pending backing to return.
      // Void means success; an empty exception means retirement is pending.
      ZuUnion<void, ZeException> close();
    
    private:
      bool send_(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length, const CommitFn &commit);
      explicit Instance(InstanceData *data) : m_data{data} { }
      InstanceData *m_data;
    };
    
    } // namespace Zxdp
    #endif /* Zxdp_HH */
    # Backend boundary
    
    This is the implementation contract supplied by the caller. It supersedes the
    earlier expanded interface in this module.
    
    Instance creation takes named parameters:
    
    * Network interface.
    * Optional network mask for packet selection. Without a mask, XDP takes over
      all traffic on the interface.
    * Head of an intrusive list of Tx pools. Each pool supplies count and packet
      size. Provision the Tx arena from that list and initialize one recycling
      free list per pool.
    * One Rx pool, with its own dedicated Rx arena.
    * Raw packet receive callback.
    
    There is no transmit-completion callback. Allocation holds one caller lease;
    accepted submission holds a separate kernel lease. Explicit pool return releases
    the caller lease, and kernel CQ or safe close releases the kernel lease. Recycle
    only when both are gone. Return may precede CQ; a caller can also retain backing
    past CQ for retransmission and return it later. Rejected send adds no kernel lease.
    One descriptor may be outstanding for an allocated slot at a time.
    
    `BufPool::writable(packet)` is a Tx-owner query with the caller allocation
    lease held. It reads the existing direct-slot lease state and becomes true
    only after kernel use retires. Use it before changing retained packet headers
    for another submission. It acquires no lease and supplies no callback, object
    association or additional bookkeeping. The caller must serialize the query,
    header writes and send on its Tx owner.
    
    The packet operations are allocation from a Tx pool, return to an Rx or Tx pool,
    and submission of a Tx packet. Application and transport object ownership is
    outside this module. The caller owns adapter composition.
    
    `send(packet, length, commit)` optionally accepts a borrowed synchronous
    `CommitFn` (`ZmFn<bool()>`). After every ordinary admission check and a successful
    Tx-ring reservation, the sole producer invokes it before changing slot ownership,
    adding the kernel lease, or publishing the descriptor. False cancels the reservation
    and returns false with no lease or descriptor. True commits the initialized
    descriptor with no further refusal. This is a publication hook, not a completion
    callback. It must not throw, retain its borrowed context, reenter Tx service, or
    perform asynchronous work. Bind a raw context pointer and `ZmFnPtr` to avoid
    allocation; a context on the caller's stack remains live through the synchronous
    call. Release-publish any caller state before returning true so a peer response
    cannot precede that state after kernel consumption. Empty hooks preserve raw send.
    
    `send()` submits and coalesces sender service on the application-assigned
    `Params::txSid`. Before scheduler startup the application configures that slot
    with `Params::txThread`, a `ZmSchedTParams` defaulting to `isolated(true)`.
    The dedicated sender calls nonblocking `sendto()` to drive kernel Tx processing.
    The caller remains the only descriptor producer and CQ owner. Descriptor
    consumption is separate from CQ retirement and never authorizes backing reuse.
    
    Submission increments a shared pending-descriptor counter before committing the
    initialized descriptor. A zero-to-one transition schedules sender service with
    `scheduler->run()` after commit. The active sender observes the kernel consumer
    cursor and tracks its unsigned delta from a persistent cursor. While no additional
    pending descriptors are visible beyond that delta, it spins for `Params::spin`
    rounds and checks shutdown. It then subtracts the observed delta atomically and
    uses the returned count to decide whether to continue. A racing publication is
    therefore retained in the count or starts a new scheduled invocation. There is
    no intentional accumulation delay and no Tx wait timeout.
    
    Tx service uses no custom scheduler wake function, epoll set or eventfd. The
    scheduler owns idle waiting after the sender returns. Rx retains its independent
    epoll/eventfd implementation described below.
    Start the scheduler before submitting packets and drain the instance before
    stopping the scheduler. After Tx production is quiescent, `stopSender()` publishes
    exit and queues a FIFO sender-slot barrier. The active loop checks exit, including
    during idle spin; the barrier clears pending state and marks sender exit before
    calling `txStopped`. Socket retirement follows that barrier. The scheduler owns
    thread startup and shutdown. Arrange CQ service independently of arrivals.
    
    All arenas, ring mappings and packet bookkeeping are allocated during setup.
    Packet storage and metadata are reused during service. Allocation and return use
    the agreed non-sharded ZmHeap payload-overlay slist. Normal sender callbacks are
    placed directly in the scheduler ring; scheduler overflow can allocate fallback
    entries. Packet admission, receive and completion resolve backing directly;
    they never search packets or buffers.
    
    The receive entry is `rx()`: process incoming packets through the configured
    callback, spin for a configurable count when idle, then use the most efficient
    suitable kernel blocking mechanism. An epoll implementation waits on packet
    readiness and an internal `eventfd`, following ZiEventLoop/ZiMultiplex. Packet
    readiness resumes processing; the call returns when explicitly woken. Expose
    `wake()` for Zutcp to interrupt the spinning or blocked receive loop and cause
    `rx()` to return. With epoll, `wake()` posts to that `eventfd` only while Rx has
    published a wait attempt; active and preposted wake pulses stay in userspace.
    No per-wakeup object is allocated. Wake observation must remain prompt during continuous traffic
    and must not be lost at the transition into epoll. The wait mechanism and its
    internal descriptors belong to this library; caller scheduling remains outside.
    
    Zutcp delegates its plugin `rx()`/`wake()` hooks to this pair. Internal driver
    NEED_WAKEUP handling and safe kernel retirement also remain in this library.
    These facilities must not grow into a second transport or application runtime.
    The public receive/wake pair owns the eventfd/epoll mechanism; raw readiness
    descriptors and a nonblocking receive-poll entry are not exposed.
    
    Current receive/wake validation covers preposted and concurrent pulses, wake
    races at epoll entry, continued receive processing after packet readiness, and
    wake during active callbacks. Full transport integration and hardware DMA
    validation remain separate work.

    # C++ language and portability
    
    Part of the repository guidance mapped in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).
    
    ## Use of C++ language
    ### Core language
    - Compile as GNU C++2b
    - DO NOT USE:
      - C++ concepts or `requires`
      - anonymous namespaces in `.cc` files (use file-scope `static`)
      - non-specific capture packs `[&]` or `[=]`
      - `enum class` or `enum T`
      - constant macros like `UINT64_C(x)` (use `uint64_t(x)` instead)
    - Use advanced C++ where it is expressive and efficient
      - Where C and C++ offer the same facility, prefer the C form:
        - Example: `#include <string.h>`, not `<cstring>`.
        - Where C99 conflicts with C++, use the GNU C++2b form.
    - Do not define pure forwarding functions to bases that do not add any logic, use `using` declarations to hoist the base definition into the derived class
    - Use `ZuLib.hh` functions in preference to STL, in particular:
      `ZuAssert`, `ZuMv`, `ZuFwd`, `ZuDecay`, `ZuDeref`, `ZuStrip`, `ZuIfT`, `ZuIsConvertible`, `ZuIsConstructible`, `ZuLaunder`, `ZuPun`, `ZuCanOverlap`
    
    ### Primitive integer types
    - use `int` and plain unadorned `unsigned` as the primary local variable integers
      - the following are static asserted in the foundational Z header `ZuLib.hh`:
        - `sizeof(int) == sizeof(unsigned)`
        - `sizeof(int) >= sizeof(int32_t)`
        - `sizeof(unsigned) >= sizeof(uint32_t)`
    - the principle is that `int` and `unsigned` will naturally match the CPU's registers
    - where 64bits is required, use `int64_t` and `uint64_t`
    - for types that might be stored in high volumes, i.e. where memory pressure may be significant, use the smallest type that spans the required range of values:
      - enums are often `int8_t` (they must be signed)
    - do NOT unnecessarily assert, for example checking that a `uint32_t` is `<= UINT_MAX`
    
    ### Static polymorphism and constraints
    - Prefer CRTP, templates, and compile-time dispatch over virtual polymorphism.
    - Use templates and CRTP to factor common code; keep logic DRY without adding weak abstractions.
    - Prefer deduced `auto` return types for functions that merely return a cast, especially CRTP accessors: `auto impl() { return static_cast<Impl *>(this); }` rather than spelling `Impl *`.
    - Express constraints with SFINAE and detector traits.
      - Keep function return types free of SFINAE expressions; put the test in a trailing `typename = ...` template parameter to avoid encoding it in every symbol.
      - Consolidate overloads that would otherwise become redeclarations with `if constexpr`, preserving their combined participation constraint and result types.
      - Generic hidden friends from different class specializations need a class-specific template discriminator; defaulted type constraints alone do not distinguish their declarations.
      - Prefer `typename = void` plus `decltype(CODE, void())` specializations to test whether `CODE` is well-formed.
      - Do not replace established `ZuIfT`/detector idioms with concepts.
      - Prefer SFINAE in function template parameters to return types, because templated return types bloat the symbol table and debug information
    - For optional CRTP callbacks, prefer side-effect-safe base defaults and direct calls such as `impl()->callback(...)`.
      - Defaults should be harmless: `return true`, `return nullptr`, or no-op.
      - Use `if constexpr` traits only when a safe base default cannot express the behavior.
    - Control inherited CRTP interfaces with access-changing `using` declarations.
      - Hide a base function with `private: using Base::X;` when the derived class encapsulates it and dependent callers must not access it directly, or when the derived class intentionally replaces it in the public interface with a new function of the same name.
      - Hoist a base function into the public interface with `public: using Base::X;`.
    
    ### ADL tagging
    - Use friend functions and ADL to tag types and expose compile-time metadata.
      - Example: `friend ZuStructPrint ZuPrintType(DB *)`; `decltype(ZuPrintType(...))` lets `ZuPrint` choose formatting.
      - Example: `ZuFields_(O *, Facet *)` lets `ZuStruct` discover fields.
    
    ### Style
    - Write idiomatic, natural, maximally expressive code for veteran C++ engineers.
    - Prefer brevity, expert idioms, and precise structure over readability for novices.
    - Do not disdain "Hacker's Delight" style when it is clear, correct, and faster.
    - Use shifts for integer multiplication and division by power-of-two literals:
      `x<<3` instead of `x*8`, and `x>>3` instead of `x/8`. For signed division,
      shift only when the value is nonnegative, since rounding otherwise differs.
    - Do not put spaces on either side of `/` in division expressions: write `x/y`.
    - `auto ptr = ...` not `auto *ptr = ...`
    - Strongly prefer `T(u)` to `static_cast<T>(u)` in all cases where they're equivalent
    
    ### Portability and compiler features
    - Target gcc and clang; use `__GNUC__`, intrinsics, `int128_t`, and `uint128_t` where appropriate.
    - Target Linux and Windows via msys2/mingw 64-bit; use `_WIN32` for Windows-specific paths.
    
    ### Enums
    - do not use `enum class` or `enum T`
      - Z **intentionally** uses enums as fully convertible with integers
        - enum values should be directly usable as compile-time array indexes, etc.
        - if a type is integral and size <= `sizeof(int)`, enum values are used in preference to `static constexpr` constants
      - if the enum needs to be type-aliased by dependents, use `struct E { enum { ... } };`
      - otherwise use `namespace E { enum { ... } };` because this permits dependents to `using namespace E`
      - above `zm` use `ZtEnum`:
        - if an external API type
        - if callers need name lookup at run-time
    
    ### Constant literals
    - when a constant literal is integral or boolean and does not need to be wider than `int`, use `enum { X = 42 };` in favor of `static constexpr T = 42`
    - Declare a compile-time string as `constexpr auto name = "text"_z`; do not
      declare a `constexpr ZuSpan`/`ZuCSpan`. `ZuString` preserves the literal's
      extent in its type, whereas a span is a non-owning run-time view. For a
      heterogeneous collection of literals, use a `constexpr` array of C-string
      pointers and construct a span only at the use boundary.
    
    ## Use of STL and other dependencies
    - minimize use of STL, BUT
    - use `iostream`, `std::cout`, `std::cerr`, `std::flush`, etc.
      - `ZuTestUtil` dependents use `log` for test diagnostics
      - do NOT use `std::cerr` for logging errors when `ZiLog` is available
      - do NOT use `Zi::stdErr()` or `Zi::stdOut()` in preference to `std::cout` or `std::cerr`
        - `Zi::std...` are only to be used for redirection when a `ZiFile` type is required
    - use `Zu` alternatives to STL: example: `ZuIfT` instead of `enable_if`
    - maximally leverage the Z framework foundation libraries:
      - `zu`, `zm`, `zt`, `zf`, `ze`, `zi`
    
    ## Windows
    - MSVC/Intel compatibility is a non-goal
    - Targets are gcc and clang under MinGW / MSYS2, 64bit only
    - do not use the `*W()` variant names, the build is always `wchar_t`-enabled:

    AM_CPPFLAGS = -I$(top_srcdir)/zu/src -I$(top_srcdir)/zm/src \

    AM_CXXFLAGS = @Z_CXXFLAGS@
    AM_LDFLAGS = @Z_LDFLAGS@ @Z_SO_LDFLAGS@
    pkginclude_HEADERS = ZxdpLib.hh Zxdp.hh ZxdpAlloc.hh
    noinst_HEADERS = ZxdpRing.hh ZxdpUMem.hh ZxdpBPF.hh ZxdpRetire.hh
    lib_LTLIBRARIES = libZxdp.la
    libZxdp_la_CPPFLAGS = $(AM_CPPFLAGS) -DZXDP_EXPORTS
    libZxdp_la_SOURCES = ZxdpLib.cc Zxdp.cc ZxdpAlloc.cc ZxdpUMem.cc ZxdpBPF.cc \

    libZxdp_la_LIBADD = $(top_builddir)/zt/src/libZt.la \
        $(top_builddir)/zm/src/libZm.la $(top_builddir)/zu/src/libZu.la \

    # Zxdp AF_XDP and DPDK backends
    
    * **Author:** Huw Rogers
    * **Date:** 2026-11-16
    * **Status:** Working hypothesis; awaiting readiness confirmation and Goldfish review.
    
    ## Overview
    
    Make `Zxdp::Instance` a virtual interface implemented by AF_XDP and DPDK.
    Remove the base class's `InstanceData *m_data`; make backend operations pure
    virtual. Add `ZtEnumNS(uint8_t, Backend, AF_XDP, DPDK)` and `Backend::T backend`
    to `Params`. Add the namespace factory `ZmRef<Instance> instance(const Params
    &params)`, which switches on `backend` and creates the corresponding derived
    instance. Use the merged AF_XDP implementation as the behavioral reference.
    
    Represent interface configuration with:
    
    ```cpp
    struct If_AF_XDP { unsigned index = 0; };
    struct If_DPDK { /* DPDK device selection; exact fields to be designed */ };
    ZuDerive(If, (ZuUnion<void, If_AF_XDP, If_DPDK>));
    ```
    
    `Params::interface` becomes `If interface = {}`. The caller supplies `txPools`
    and singular `rxPool`; these determine packet storage and ring provisioning.
    Do not duplicate that provisioning in `If_DPDK`.
    
    ## Analysis
    
    The merged baseline has separate caller and submission leases, a borrowed
    synchronous send commit hook, a scheduler sender slot, receive/wake service,
    queue telemetry and explicit sender shutdown. The backend abstraction must
    account for this complete API rather than the earlier AF_XDP interface.
    
    The main technical questions for review are whether DPDK can preserve the
    commit hook's no-refusal-after-true guarantee, how driver ownership releases
    submission leases, and how caller-held packet backing survives close. A
    successful transmit burst alone must not be treated as proof that backing
    can be reused. Pool recycling and writable queries must follow actual ownership.
    
    DPDK receive waiting also needs examination: the software ring tests must
    exercise prompt, counted wakes without assuming every driver supplies an
    AF_XDP-style packet readiness descriptor. Pool provisioning must account for
    driver descriptor requirements without introducing duplicate public sizing.
    
    The tagged interface and explicit backend can disagree. Their validation and
    the behavior of an unset interface must be specified. The current factory's
    error string and retained handle for pending rollback must be reconciled with
    the requested one-argument namespace factory.
    
    ## Goals vs. Non-Goals
    
    * **In-Scope Goals:** Virtual Instance API; backend enum and factory; tagged
      interface parameters; AF_XDP and DPDK implementations in zxdp; migration of
      affected callers; DPDK software tests using the arrangements documented in
      `dpdk_loopback.md`; preservation of packet ownership and service contracts.
    * **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:** A transport stack or application runtime;
      duplicate ring sizing in `If_DPDK`; claims of physical NIC DMA, offload or
      wire-latency validation from software tests.
    
    ## Alternatives Weighed
    
    * Rejected by author: configuring ring setup separately in `If_DPDK`.
      Ring provisioning comes from `txPools` and `rxPool`.
    * Rejected by author: interpreting `rxPools` as multiple receive pools.
      That spelling was a typo; retain singular `rxPool`.
    
    ## Key Decisions & Staging for Next Steps
    
    Confirmed decisions are the virtual backend boundary, explicit backend
    selection, tagged interface configuration, pool-driven provisioning and
    software DPDK testing. No implementation changes have been made.
    
    Review must resolve the exact DPDK device selector, process-wide EAL ownership,
    factory failure reporting, completion tracking, receive idle behavior and any
    backend-specific treatment of scheduler sender service. These are design
    questions, not additional configuration requested from the author.
    
    Use `net_ring` for in-process packet loopback and `net_pcap` for deterministic
    capture input/output where appropriate. Test pool exhaustion, rejected send,
    commit cancellation, ownership through completion and close, wake races and
    repeated teardown as well as packet contents. Physical hardware validation
    remains separate.
    
    References: [DPDK ring driver](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/nics/ring.html),
    [DPDK PCAP/ring drivers](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides-25.03/nics/pcap_ring.html),
    [EAL parameters](https://doc.dpdk.org/guides-25.11/linux_gsg/linux_eal_parameters.html),
    and the repository's `dpdk_loopback.md` and `zxdp/INTERFACE.md`.

    ---
    name: egm-synthesizer
    description: Intermediate Swarm Compiler and Aggregator coordinating parallel Goldfish reviewers, deduplicating findings, and compiling deliverable reports.

    # Core Mandates (Swarm Compiler & Output Synthesizer)
    
    You are the **EGM Synthesizer Persona**. You serve as an intermediate orchestrator and technical compiler between the root agent (the Elephant) and the swarm of stateless Goldfish subagents.
    
    1. **Subagent Delegation**: When requested by the Elephant, you spawn and coordinate the individual Goldfish subagents using your harness's subagent tool.
    2. **Output Offloading & Normalization**: The Goldfish subagents report raw findings in unconstrained natural language. You take full responsibility for normalizing their feedback, deduplicating overlapping points, grouping findings by severity (🔴 Blocker, 🟡 Major, 🟢 Nit), and normalizing file line references.
    3. **Artifact-First Delivery**: You format the consolidated feedback into a polished Markdown document and write it directly to the workspace or artifact directory using your file-writing tool.
    4. **Clean Handoff**: You send a single, concise completion message back to the Elephant with the artifact link or path.
    
    ---
    
    # Role
    
    You are **EGM Synthesizer**.
    You are an expert Multi-Agent Coordinator and Technical Editor. You bridge the gap between divergent, specialized Goldfish analyzers and the high-level Elephant partner by transforming raw, multi-perspective feedback into a structured, unified deliverable.
    
    ---
    
    # Instructions
    
    Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller (`Mode: BRAINSTORM` vs `Mode: REVIEW`):
    
    ## IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)
    1. **Subagent Spawning**: Launch the parallel Goldfish swarm across the 7 specialized lenses (`design_critic`, `codebase_details`, `zoom_out`, `comprehension`, `implementation_readiness`, `structural`, `inventive_catalyst`), passing `Mode: BRAINSTORM` and `FeatureConcept: [FeatureConcept]`. Set role titles ending in `-Brainstormer` (e.g., `Skeptical Architect Brainstormer`, `UX & Ergonomics Brainstormer`, `Inventive Catalyst Brainstormer`).
       * **Failed Reviewers**: A reviewer that times out, fails, or returns no report did not review. Retry it once. If it fails again, its status is `not run` in `concepts_brief.md`. Never count it as a lens with zero findings.
    2. **Aggregate & Synthesize Concept Brief**: Collect findings from all 7 Goldfish, deduplicate overlapping points, synthesize inventive contradictions and pattern resolutions alongside risk dimensions, and compile them into `concepts_brief.md`.
    3. **Write Deliverable**: Write the synthesized brief to `concepts_brief.md` using your file-writing tool.
    4. **Notify Elephant**: Send a completion message to the Elephant with the `concepts_brief.md` path.
    
    ## IF Mode: REVIEW (Document Audit)
    * **Personas Directory**: `agents/{name}.md`
    * **Document Standards Directory**: `resources/document_standards/{standard_name}.md`
    
    1. **Subagent Spawning**: Launch the requested subagents in the `Reviewers` list (optionally launching two independent instances, A and B, for each reviewer to maximize finding recall and eliminate non-deterministic evaluation gaps).
       * **Failed Reviewers**: A reviewer that times out, fails, or returns no report did not review. Retry it once. If it fails again, its status is `not run`. Never count it as a reviewer with zero findings.
    2. **Aggregate & Triage**: Group reported findings from all subagent instances into 🔴 **Blocker**, 🟡 **Major**, and 🟢 **Nit**. Deduplicate overlapping findings and normalize file references.
    3. **Format Review Report**: Format the consolidated findings according to this Markdown layout:
    
       ```markdown
       # Goldfish Review Report
    
       **Target:** `[TargetFile]` (`[LineRange]`)
    
       ## Reviewer Status
    
       | Reviewer | Status |
       | --- | --- |
       | `[agent-shortname]` | [completed \| not run] |
    
       ## Prioritized Findings (Blockers -> Major -> Nits)
    
       ### [Issue Name] - Severity: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
       * **Reviewer Lens:** `[agent-shortname]`
       * **Affected Scope:** `[Lines Start-End]` (or section header)
       * **Discrepancy Description**: [Precise technical, structural, or clarity gap.]
       * **Rationale & Recommendation**: [Concise, objective reason and guidance.]
       ```
    
    4. **Write Artifact**: Write findings to the report file the caller names (`goldfish_review_report.md` if none) using your file-writing tool.
    5. **Notify Elephant**: Send a completion message to the Elephant with the status (`completed` or `not run`) of each requested reviewer, the severity breakdown, and the artifact link.

    # Output Format
    
    Always produce the deliverable artifact file (`goldfish_review_report.md` or `concepts_brief.md`) before sending the completion notification back to the primary agent.
    # Harnesses
    
    EGM is one set of skills and personas. This repository serves as the
    plugin source for each supported harness. No harness gets a fork of the skill
    text.
    
    ## Install
    
    | Harness | Install |
    | --- | --- |
    | ChatGPT desktop | Install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357) (desktop-only listing); see [packaging](codex.md#test-a-local-package) for personal testing |
    | Codex desktop | Install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357) (desktop-only listing) |
    | Antigravity CLI | `agy plugin install https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model` |
    | Antigravity App | Run `/plugin` or see [installation instructions](#antigravity-app-and-antigravity-for-ides) |
    | Antigravity for IDEs | Run `/plugin` or see [installation instructions](#antigravity-app-and-antigravity-for-ides) |
    | Antigravity IDE (standalone) | Not supported; see [installation instructions](#antigravity-app-and-antigravity-for-ides) |
    | Claude Code | `claude plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model && claude plugin install egm@egm` |
    | Claude Cowork | Install from claude.ai/plugins or the Cowork plugin panel via marketplace `google/elephant-goldfish-model` |
    | Codex CLI | `codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model && codex plugin add egm@egm` |
    | ChatGPT workspace import | Admin > Plugins > Add > Import marketplace, repo URL `https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model`, path `.agents/plugins`; cloud review limits still apply |

    Install the whole plugin. Skill-only installers that copy `skills/` alone
    break EGM, because the skills read `agents/` and
    `resources/document_standards/` at run time.
    
    ### Antigravity App and Antigravity for IDEs
    
    - **Antigravity App**: Run `/plugin`, ask the agent `Install https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model`, or manually install into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/` using the commands below.
    - **Antigravity for IDEs (Extension for Visual Studio Code)**: Run `/plugin`, ask the agent `Install https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model`, or manually install into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/` using the commands below.
    - **Antigravity IDE (Standalone)**: Not supported at this time. Although the plugin and skills load from `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/`, standalone Antigravity IDE (tested on macOS and Linux) does not expose the fresh-context subagent tool (`invoke_subagent`) required for Goldfish reviews (`/egm-brainstorm` and `/egm-review`).
    
    The Antigravity App and Antigravity for IDEs share the global plugin directory
    `~/.gemini/config/plugins/<name>/`. For a fresh manual installation without the
    `agy` CLI, copy the full runtime bundle into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/`
    (copying into an existing plugin directory can leave obsolete files behind, so
    remove `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm` first when updating):
    
    ```sh
    git clone https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model.git
    cd elephant-goldfish-model
    mkdir -p ~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm
    cp -R plugin.json README.md LICENSE skills agents resources docs assets ~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/
    ```
    
    Reload the window (or restart the Antigravity App), then confirm that `egm`
    appears in the plugin list and that its skills (`egm-brainstorm`, `egm-draft`,
    `egm-review`) are available. The command form for these skills in the
    Antigravity App and Antigravity for IDEs has not been verified.
    
    ## Manifests
    
    Root `plugin.json` is the canonical source for plugin identity, version,
    description, and publisher metadata. It follows the portable Agent Plugins
    1.0.0 format; the `$schema` key is omitted because omp routes manifests that
    declare it to a strict validator that rejects `disable-model-invocation`.
    Update shared values there first, then update the compatibility
    manifests; unit tests reject metadata drift. Keep platform-specific fields in
    their existing manifests until installation tests justify removing them.
    
    Marketplace files are discovery catalogs pointing to this package, not copies
    of its skills. In particular, `.agents/plugins/` contains the Codex catalog,
    while `agents/` contains reviewer personas. All hosts share the same `skills/`,
    `agents/`, and `resources/` content.
    
    | Harness | Manifest | Skills | Subagents |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | Antigravity | `plugin.json` | `skills/` (default) | `agents/` (default) |
    | Claude Code | `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` | `skills/` (default) | Claude adapters and orchestrators listed in `plugin.json` `agents` |
    | Claude Cowork | `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` | `skills/` (default) | Subagents run inside Cowork; hooks n/a |
    | Codex | `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` | `skills` path | Not shipped; general-purpose subagent reads the persona file |
    | ChatGPT | `plugin.json`, `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`; `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` for workspace import | `skills` path | Detect native tools in the current session; general-purpose agent reads the persona |
    | omp | `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (Claude-compatible fallback) | `skills/` (default) | Personas from `agents/`/`.claude-plugin/agents/` register as native `task` agents |
    | Muse | `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (Claude-compatible fallback) | `skills/` (default) | 10 adapters import as agents; tool projections unsupported |
    
    Persona prompts live in `agents/`, the directory Antigravity
    scans for subagents. Each persona has `name` and `description` frontmatter, so
    harnesses that load `agents/*.md` register them as named subagents
    (`egm-design`, `egm-zoom-out`, and so on).
    
    When you add a reviewer persona, add a Claude adapter under
    `.claude-plugin/agents/` and list it in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`.
    The adapter reads the shared persona and sets Claude's read-only tools and
    context isolation. This avoids imposing Claude tool names on other hosts.
    In Claude Code, `/plugin` > Errors will report that the default `agents/` folder is ignored because the manifest sets `"agents"`; this warning is expected and harmless (see [Claude integration](claude.md#claude-code-warning-default-agents-folder-is-ignored)).
    
    ## Delegation
    
    Skills say "spawn a subagent" and name a persona. Each harness maps that
    phrase to its own tool:
    
    | Harness | Subagent tool | Named personas | Nesting |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | Antigravity | `invoke_subagent` | Yes | Yes |
    | Claude Code | Agent (Task) tool | Yes | Up to 3 levels by default |
    | Claude Cowork | Cowork subagents | Yes | Subagents run inside Cowork |
    | Codex | Native spawn/wait tools; inspect the available schema | No | Detect at runtime; direct dispatch fallback |
    | ChatGPT | Native spawn/wait tools when exposed by the current Work session | No | Detect at runtime; direct dispatch fallback |
    | omp | `task` tool | Yes | Yes |
    | Muse | Native subagents; inspect the available schema | Named spawn rejected in 1.4.14; general-purpose fallback verified | Detect at runtime; direct dispatch fallback |
    
    Where a harness has no named persona, the skill spawns a general-purpose
    subagent and tells it to read `agents/<file>.md` first. If a harness cannot
    nest subagents, use direct dispatch instead of the synthesizer.
    
    A Goldfish review needs a fresh context. If a harness has no subagent tool,
    the review skills stop instead of running in the same context. Check actual
    tool availability rather than inferring it from the product name. This applies
    to standalone Antigravity IDE and to ChatGPT modes that do not expose native
    fresh-context delegation.
    
    Fresh conversation context does not mean that the host omits its instruction
    files. Codex's `fork_context: false` and `fork_turns: "none"` isolate parent
    turns; they do not establish that project or user instructions are excluded.
    Keep stable workspace conventions in instruction files. State review
    assumptions that the Goldfish must challenge as explicit review criteria.
    
    ## Artifact Directory
    
    Skills write briefs, drafts, and reports to the working directory, or to the
    harness's artifact directory if it has one. In Claude Code, Claude Cowork,
    Codex, and ChatGPT, you can name another folder. Add this line to your prompt,
    or to an agent instructions file that your harness loads (`CLAUDE.md` or
    `AGENTS.md`, in the project or at user level):
    
    ```text
    EGM artifact directory: .dev/docs
    ```
    
    A relative path is relative to the working directory. If a path set in an
    instructions file resolves outside the working directory, after following
    symbolic links, EGM asks you to confirm it before creating the folder or
    writing there. If you decline or no one can confirm, as in a headless run, the
    files go to the working directory. The answer isn't saved, so a new session
    asks again. A path in your prompt needs no confirmation. Design docs and other
    project files do not move. Claude Code reads a project `AGENTS.md` only when
    the project has no `CLAUDE.md`.
    
    Commit approved specifications in `docs/designs/` and project rules in
    `AGENTS.md`. Teammates and agents then use the same committed files. Add
    `.dev/docs` to `.gitignore` only to keep scratch drafts out of git before
    approval.
    
    ## Support Status & Contributing Other Harnesses
    
    **Antigravity CLI**, **Claude Code**, and **Codex** pass automated installation
    and end-to-end workflow fixtures. Reviewer isolation evidence is narrower:
    parent-turn isolation and host-instruction exclusion are separate results.
    
    Claude reviewer adapters set `omitClaudeMd: true`; see the
    [Claude integration](claude.md#reviewer-isolation). For Codex, issue [#237](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/237)
    reports that Codex CLI 0.166.0 supplied project and user `AGENTS.md` files
    despite `fork_turns: "none"`. For Antigravity CLI, the same issue reports
    project `AGENTS.md` and `GEMINI.md` in reviewer context. These are reported
    host-instruction leaks, not evidence that parent conversation turns leaked.
    The Codex test and recorded Antigravity run check parent-turn isolation only;
    neither verifies instruction-file exclusion. No host-specific exclusion
    control is verified here for Codex or Antigravity.
    
    **Claude Cowork** ([#105](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/105)) and **ChatGPT Work** ([#106](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/106)) have working installation paths with open cloud trace verification gaps. The README's prefix guidance covers only Antigravity (agy CLI), Claude Code, and Codex. For ChatGPT workspace imports, the skills are reached through `@egm` (see [ChatGPT](codex.md#chatgpt)); the command form in Claude Cowork is not recorded yet.
    
    **omp** ([#186](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/186)) has a working installation path. Skills are invoked as `/skill:egm-<command>` (omp registers one command per skill; it has no `/egm-*` namespace). Community-verified on omp v18.12.6: all seven skills discover and resolve, and all nine reviewer personas register as subagents. End-to-end workflow fixtures are not yet automated for omp.
    
    **Muse** (1.4.14) has a working installation path. `muse plugins validate` reports the plugin valid with all seven skills and all ten agent adapters supported; every agent tool projection is unsupported, so Claude tool allowlists do not restrict Muse reviewers. Install from a local path; `marketplace add` on this repository discovers zero plugins because Muse reads the Codex catalog first. End-to-end workflow fixtures passed on 2026-10-30 (brainstorm, draft, and uninterrupted review with 15 fresh-context reviewers); named `egm/egm-*` agents cannot be spawned in this runtime, so reviewers used the general-purpose fallback reading the installed persona first. See the [Muse guide](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/docs/muse.md). No skill routes a Muse session to that guide yet ([#252](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/252)), so point the session at it.
    
    **Windsurf** (renamed Devin Desktop on 2026-06-02; [#376](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/376)) has experimental workspace routing. The rule and workflow files resolve the shared `skills/*/SKILL.md`, `agents/*.md`, and `resources/document_standards/*.md` files directly. They do not copy skill text. Goldfish reviews stop if fresh-context, read-only subagent delegation is unavailable, and reviewers launch on the host's read-only subagent profile. Devin CLI 3000.12.43 runs on 2026-11-10 passed routing, human pauses, read-only reviewers, and parent-marker isolation with every file write denied, so no workflow ran to a final artifact. Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI run the same agent, Devin Local, which replaced Cascade. The Devin Desktop IDE remains untested. The CLI does not list `.windsurf/workflows/` as slash commands; `/egm-*` requests route through the rule. Denying a permission prompt ends the host's turn without a message; send a follow-up message to continue. See the [design](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/docs/designs/windsurf_support.md#recorded-cli-evidence-2026-11-10) for the evidence.
    
    See the [harness test record](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/TESTING.md#harness-test-record) for tested surfaces and limits.
    
    We welcome contributors who want to help verify and expand harness support.
    
    ### Contributing Support for New Harnesses
    
    A harness counts as supported after `/egm-brainstorm`, `/egm-draft`, and
    `/egm-review` run end to end through its plugin install. When contributing
    support for another harness:
    
    1. Add the appropriate manifest or configuration file to the repository root
       (e.g., matching the harness's plugin/extension standard).
    2. Document install steps, manifest mapping, and delegation mechanics in this guide
       (`docs/harnesses.md`).
    3. Verify that `/egm-brainstorm`, `/egm-draft`, and `/egm-review` run end to end,
       and attach verification notes or execution transcripts in your Pull Request description
       (as outlined in the [Pull Request Template](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)).

    ZmRef<Instance> Instance::create(Params params, ZtString<> &error)
    {
      auto mask = params.netmask;
      ZmRef<InstanceData> instance = new InstanceData{ZuMv(params)};
      if (instance->init(mask, error)) return instance;
      auto cause = ZuMv(error);
      ZtString<> cleanup;
      if (!instance->close(cleanup) && instance->state != InstanceData::Closed) {
        error = ZuMv(cause);
        error << "; rollback pending: " << cleanup;
        return instance;
      }
      error = ZuMv(cause);
      return nullptr;
    }
    Instance::~Instance() = default;
    unsigned Instance::allQueues(Ztc::QueueMgr::AllFn fn) const
    {
      ZmGuard guard(m_data->queueLock);
      unsigned count = 0;
      for (auto queue : m_data->queues) {
        if (!queue) continue;
        auto &socket = queue->socket;
        fn(&socket.rx()); fn(&socket.fill()); fn(&socket.tx()); fn(&socket.comp());
        count += 4;
      }
      return count;
    }
    bool Instance::ready() const { return m_data->state == InstanceData::Active; }
    unsigned Instance::ifindex() const { return m_data->interface; }
    unsigned Instance::mtu() const { return m_data->link.mtu; }
    bool Instance::zeroCopy() const {
      auto queue = m_data->queues.length() ? m_data->queues[0] : nullptr;
      return queue && queue->socket.zeroCopy();
    }
    ZuBSpan Instance::mac() const { return m_data->link.mac; }
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Instance::close()
    {
      ZtString<> error;
      if (m_data->close(error)) return {};
      if (!error) return ZeException{};
      return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", ([error = ZuMv(error)](auto &s) {
        s << error;
      }));
    }
    bool Instance::stopSender() { return m_data->stopSender(); }
    
    bool Instance::send(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length, const CommitFn &commit)
      { return send_(packet, length, commit); }
    
    bool Instance::send_(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length, const CommitFn &commit)
    {
      if (!ready() || !packet || !length) return false;
      auto pool = m_data->arena->pool(packet);
      if (!pool || pool == m_data->rxPool) return false;
      auto id = pool->slot(packet);
      if (id == BufPool::NoSlot) return false;
      auto canonical = pool->backing(id);
      auto wire = unsigned(packet - canonical);
      if (length > pool->size - wire) return false;
      auto &slot = m_data->arena->txSlot(*pool, id);
      if (slot.pending) return false;
      auto &ring = m_data->queues[0]->socket.tx();
      if (m_data->txHeld == ring.count() || !ring.reserve(1)) return false;
      // No callback may retain this borrowed context or reenter Tx service.
      // Its accepted publication precedes the descriptor release store below.
      if (commit && !commit()) { ring.cancel(); return false; }
      slot.wire = wire;
      slot.active = m_data->txHeld;
      m_data->txActive[m_data->txHeld++] = canonical;
      slot.pending = true;
      ++slot.refs;
      auto address = uint64_t(packet - m_data->arena->data());
      ring.entry(0) = {address, length, 0};
      bool idle = !m_data->txPending++;
      ring.commit();
      if (idle) m_data->scheduler->run([data = m_data] { data->serveTx(); }, m_data->txSid);
      return true;
    }
    
    void Instance::wake() { m_data->notify(); }
