    # Backend boundary
    
    This is the implementation contract supplied by the caller. It supersedes the
    earlier expanded interface in this module.
    
    Select the cold backend with `Zxdp::instance(Zxdp::Type::Xdp)`. `Instance` is
    a polymorphic interface; its virtual `init(const Params &)` dispatches a tagged
    union of backend configurations. Construct its payload in place:
    
    ```cpp
    Zxdp::Params config(
      Zxdp::Params::New<Zxdp::Params::Index<Zxdp::Xdp::Params>{}>{});
    auto &params = config.p<Zxdp::Xdp::Params>();
    ```
    
    `Xdp::Params` inherits common `Params_` fields
    and adds `ifindex`, `netmask`, `txSid` and `txThread`. Assign fields directly.
    Initialization takes:
    
    * Network interface index (`Xdp::Params::ifindex`).
    * Optional network mask for packet selection. Without a mask, XDP takes over
      all traffic on the interface.
    * An owning `Zi::IOBufPoolList` of Tx pools. Each pool supplies
      count, packet size and alignment. Provision the Tx arena from that list and
      initialize one recycling free list per pool.
    * One unlinked `ZmRef<Zi::IOBufPool>` Rx pool, with its own dedicated Rx arena.
    * Raw packet receive callback.
    
    Zxdp depends on Zi. `instance->bufPool(count, size, headRoom, tailRoom, align)`
    returns `ZmRef<Zi::IOBufPool>` implementing allocation/return over registered
    arena slots. The concrete implementation is internal; generic Zi pools cannot
    provide the required arena bookkeeping. Headroom and tailroom default to zero,
    alignment to 64 bytes. Use the same pool directly with Zi's typed metadata
    allocator. Add nodes to `Params_::txPools` with `pushNode()`, or move in an existing
    list. A node belongs to one owning list at a time. Populate `Xdp::Params` in the
    generic `Params` union and pass that union by const reference to init. The backend
    retains one reference per pool through close; intrusive membership remains only
    in the caller configuration list.
    Freeze pool geometry through active service. Retain a pool reference for packets
    that outlive the instance.
    
    `instance->init(config)` returns `ZuUnion<void, ZeException>`. An exception
    reports the setup cause without discarding the instance. Always retain that
    instance until close finishes, including rollback after failed initialization.
    `close()` returns `ZuUnion<bool, ZeException>`: `true` means fully closed,
    `false` means retirement is pending, and the exception branch reports an actual
    failure. Pending retirement is not an empty exception.
    
    There is no transmit-completion callback. Allocation holds one caller lease;
    accepted submission holds a separate kernel lease. Explicit pool return releases
    the caller lease, and kernel CQ or safe close releases the kernel lease. Recycle
    only when both are gone. Return may precede CQ; a caller can also retain backing
    past CQ for retransmission and return it later. Rejected send adds no kernel lease.
    One descriptor may be outstanding for an allocated slot at a time.
    
    `Zi::IOBufPool::writable(packet)` is a Tx-owner query with the caller allocation
    lease held. It reads the existing direct-slot lease state and becomes true
    only after kernel use retires. Use it before changing retained packet headers
    for another submission. It acquires no lease and supplies no callback, object
    association or additional bookkeeping. The caller must serialize the query,
    header writes and send on its Tx owner.
    
    The packet operations are allocation from a Tx pool, return to an Rx or Tx pool,
    and submission of a Tx packet. Application and transport object ownership is
    outside this module. The caller owns adapter composition.
    
    `bool send(uint8_t *packet, unsigned length)` returns true for accepted
    submission. False acquires no kernel lease, publishes no descriptor and leaves
    backing with the caller. After true the packet must remain immutable until
    kernel retirement; the independent caller lease may be returned before or after
    that retirement.
    
    `send()` submits and coalesces sender service on the application-assigned
    `Xdp::Params::txSid`. Before scheduler startup the application configures that slot
    with `Xdp::Params::txThread`, a `ZmSchedTParams` defaulting to `isolated(true)`.
    The dedicated sender calls nonblocking `sendto()` to drive kernel Tx processing.
    The caller remains the only descriptor producer and CQ owner. Descriptor
    consumption is separate from CQ retirement and never authorizes backing reuse.
    
    Submission increments a shared pending-descriptor counter before committing the
    initialized descriptor. A zero-to-one transition schedules sender service with
    `scheduler->run()` after commit. The active sender observes the kernel consumer
    cursor and tracks its unsigned delta from a persistent cursor. While no additional
    pending descriptors are visible beyond that delta, it spins for `Params_::spin`
    rounds and checks shutdown. It then subtracts the observed delta atomically and
    uses the returned count to decide whether to continue. A racing publication is
    therefore retained in the count or starts a new scheduled invocation. There is
    no intentional accumulation delay and no Tx wait timeout.
    
    Tx service uses no custom scheduler wake function, epoll set or eventfd. The
    scheduler owns idle waiting after the sender returns. Rx retains its independent
    epoll/eventfd implementation described below.
    Start the scheduler before submitting packets and drain the instance before
    stopping the scheduler. After Tx production is quiescent, `stopTx()` publishes
    exit and queues a FIFO sender-slot barrier. The active loop checks exit, including
    during idle spin; the barrier clears pending state and marks sender exit before
    calling `txStopped`. Socket retirement follows that barrier. The scheduler owns
    thread startup and shutdown. Arrange CQ service independently of arrivals.
    
    All arenas, ring mappings and packet bookkeeping are allocated during setup.
    Packet storage and metadata are reused during service. Allocation and return use
    the agreed non-sharded ZmHeap payload-overlay slist. Normal sender callbacks are
    placed directly in the scheduler ring; scheduler overflow can allocate fallback
    entries. Packet admission, receive and completion resolve backing directly;
    they never search packets or buffers.
    
    The receive entry is `rx()`: process incoming packets through the configured
    callback, spin for a configurable count when idle, then use the most efficient
    suitable kernel blocking mechanism. An epoll implementation waits on packet
    readiness and an internal `eventfd`, following ZiEventLoop/ZiMultiplex. Packet
    readiness resumes processing; the call returns when explicitly woken. Expose
    `wake()` for Zutcp to interrupt the spinning or blocked receive loop and cause
    `rx()` to return. With epoll, `wake()` posts to that `eventfd` only while Rx has
    published a wait attempt; active and preposted wake pulses stay in userspace.
    No per-wakeup object is allocated. Wake observation must remain prompt during continuous traffic
    and must not be lost at the transition into epoll. The wait mechanism and its
    internal descriptors belong to this library; caller scheduling remains outside.
    
    Zutcp delegates its plugin `rx()`/`wake()` hooks to this pair. Internal driver
    NEED_WAKEUP handling and safe kernel retirement also remain in this library.
    These facilities must not grow into a second transport or application runtime.
    The public receive/wake pair owns the eventfd/epoll mechanism; raw readiness
    descriptors and a nonblocking receive-poll entry are not exposed.
    
    Current receive/wake validation covers preposted and concurrent pulses, wake
    races at epoll entry, continued receive processing after packet readiness, and
    wake during active callbacks. Full transport integration and hardware DMA
    validation remain separate work.
    # Zxdp raw packet service
    
    ## Overview
    
    Linux AF_XDP packet allocation, receive/transmit service, XDP program attachment, and kernel retirement. Application transport composition and thread scheduling belong to callers.
    
    ## Interface
    
    - [Zxdp.hh](./Zxdp.hh): `Params` is a tagged union; `Xdp::Params` selects interface index, optional destination CIDR, intrusive Tx pools, dedicated Rx pool, receive callback, and spin count. `instance(Type::Xdp)` selects a cold polymorphic `Instance` exposing union-dispatched `init(const Params &)` after in-place payload construction with `Params::New<Params::Index<Xdp::Params>{}>{}`, readiness/MTU/MAC/zero-copy queries, `send`, `rx`, `wake`, `pollTx`, and retryable `close`; there is no transmit-completion callback.
    - [ZxdpPool.hh](./ZxdpPool.hh): internal `Xdp::BufPool` implements `Zi::IOBufPool`; callers obtain owning pool references through the selected instance's virtual `bufPool`.
    - [Makefile.am](./Makefile.am): exports `libZxdp.la` and installs `ZxdpLib.hh` and `Zxdp.hh`; pool, ring, arena, BPF, and retirement headers are private. `init` and `warmup` have empty implementations in [ZxdpLib.cc](./ZxdpLib.cc).
    - Internal `Xdp::Ring` views manage checked reservations; `Xdp::UMem` and `Xdp::Xsk` manage backing and socket registration; `Xdp::KernelRetirement` reports `Error`, `Pending`, or `Done`; `Xdp::Filter`, `Xdp::BPFProgram`, and `Xdp::BPFAttach` implement selection and attachment. [ZxdpRing.hh](./ZxdpRing.hh), [ZxdpUMem.hh](./ZxdpUMem.hh), [ZxdpRetire.hh](./ZxdpRetire.hh), [ZxdpBPF.hh](./ZxdpBPF.hh)
    
    ## Invariants
    
    - `Instance` requires separate single Rx and Tx owners. Allocation/free may run elsewhere. Accepted sends hold a kernel lease independently of the caller allocation lease; backing is recycled only after both end. Bytes remain immutable until kernel retirement. Rejection acquires no kernel lease; only one descriptor may be pending per slot. [Zxdp.hh](./Zxdp.hh), [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc), [ZxdpPool.cc](./ZxdpPool.cc)
    - Initialization retains its own reference per pool through close; intrusive membership remains only in the caller configuration list. Retain a pool reference for packets that outlive the instance, and freeze links/count/size while bound. `Xdp::BufPool` destruction asserts no used slots. `Xdp::UMem::create` requires unused pools, an owning Tx list, supported power-of-two page geometry and bounded fitting counts/sizes. [ZxdpPool.hh](./ZxdpPool.hh), [ZxdpUMem.cc](./ZxdpUMem.cc)
    - Before `Instance::close`, wake/join Rx and quiesce Tx and wake callers. Retain the selected instance after init failure until rollback and close finish. `Xdp::KernelRetirement` requires original/probe objects and packet holds until `Done`; an `Error` does not authorize release. Closing an XSK descriptor alone does not establish DMA retirement. [Zxdp.hh](./Zxdp.hh), [ZxdpRetire.hh](./ZxdpRetire.hh), [ZxdpUMem.hh](./ZxdpUMem.hh)
    - `Instance::init` requires interface, Rx pool, callback, no pre-existing XDP program, and enough Rx buffers for all queues. `Xdp::Ring::mapLength` requires safe aligned nonoverlapping offsets and a power-of-two count; mapping lifetime is external and reservations cannot overlap. [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc), [ZxdpRing.hh](./ZxdpRing.hh)
    
    ## Side Effects
    
    - `Instance::init` provisions arenas/bookkeeping, epoll/eventfd, BPF maps/programs and queue sockets; `Xdp::UMem::create` mmaps writable backing; `Xdp::Xsk::prepare` opens AF_XDP sockets and maps rings. Kernel calls can fail; the library does not acquire privileges. [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc), [ZxdpUMem.cc](./ZxdpUMem.cc)
    - `Xdp::BufPool::init` overlays freelist links on payload backing. `send` publishes the submitted arena address, records canonical backing plus wire offset, and may kick the kernel. `pollTx` consumes at most 64 CQ entries, matches pending slots by wire offset excluding bit zero (the Linux generic-Tx destructor tag), releases matched kernel leases, and returns the number retired. Unmatched entries are consumed without incrementing that result. [ZxdpPool.cc](./ZxdpPool.cc), [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc)
    - `Instance::rx` services queues, spins then blocks in epoll, and invokes receive callbacks on arena bytes. The backend wake notifier records a persistent wake pulse and writes eventfd; one pulse ends one receive invocation, including preposted pulses. [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc)
    - `Xdp::classifierCode` supports destination IPv4/IPv6 filtering through two VLAN headers. Nonmatching/truncated filtered frames pass; selected frames redirect by Rx queue with a drop fallback. An empty filter selects all traffic. Attachment uses guarded program identity and driver-to-SKB fallback only on explicit unsupported-operation rejection; detach preserves foreign programs. [ZxdpBPF.cc](./ZxdpBPF.cc)
    - `Instance::close` removes destinations and retires one queue per call before bounded buffer return and descriptor/program cleanup. `Xdp::KernelRetirement::retry` probes rebinding with an empty observer: busy remains pending, successful binding establishes retirement. Arena destruction unmaps backing. [Zxdp.cc](./Zxdp.cc), [ZxdpRetire.cc](./ZxdpRetire.cc), [ZxdpUMem.cc](./ZxdpUMem.cc)

    namespace Zxdp::Xdp {
    
    BufPool::BufPool(unsigned n, unsigned bytes) {
      count = n;
      size = bytes;
    }
    BufPool::~BufPool() { ZmAssert_(!unsigned(m_used)); }
    
    void BufPool::init(
      ZmRef<UMem> arena, uint64_t offset, unsigned stride, unsigned prefix, unsigned first)
    {
      ZmAssert_(!unsigned(m_used));
      m_active = 0;
      m_arena = ZuMv(arena);
      m_offset = offset;
      m_shift = __builtin_ctz(stride);
      m_prefix = prefix;
      m_first = first;
      m_tx = offset >= m_arena->layout().rxLength;
      m_head = 0;
      // Same non-sharded payload-overlay slist initialization as ZmHeap arenas.
      for (unsigned i = count; i; --i) {
        auto p = backing(i - 1);
        reinterpret_cast<ZmAtomic<uintptr_t> *>(p)->store_(m_head.load_());
        m_head.store_(uintptr_t(p));
      }
      m_active = 1;
    }
    
    uint8_t *BufPool::alloc()
    {
      if (ZuUnlikely(!unsigned(m_active))) return nullptr;
      uintptr_t p;
    loop:
      p = m_head.load_();
      if (ZuUnlikely(!p)) return nullptr;
      if (ZuUnlikely(p & 1)) { ZmAtomic_acquire(); goto loop; }
      if (ZuUnlikely(m_head.cmpXch(p | 1, p) != p)) goto loop;
      ++m_used;
      m_head = reinterpret_cast<ZmAtomic<uintptr_t> *>(p)->load_();
      if (m_tx) m_arena->txSlot(*this, slot(reinterpret_cast<void *>(p))).refs = 1;
      return reinterpret_cast<uint8_t *>(p);
    }
    
    void BufPool::free(uint8_t *packet)
    {
      auto id = slot(packet);
      ZmAssert_(id != NoSlot);
      if (m_tx && --m_arena->txSlot(*this, id).refs) return;
      auto p = backing(id);
      uintptr_t next;
    loop:
      next = m_head.load_();
      if (next & 1) { ZmAtomic_acquire(); goto loop; }
      reinterpret_cast<ZmAtomic<uintptr_t> *>(p)->store_(next);
      if (m_head.cmpXch(uintptr_t(p), next) != next) goto loop;
      // Final accounting follows publication; no mapping access follows it.
      ZmAssert_(m_used--);
    }
    
    unsigned BufPool::slot(const void *packet) const
    {
      if (!m_arena) return NoSlot;
      auto begin = uintptr_t(m_arena->data()) + m_offset + m_prefix;
      auto address = uintptr_t(packet);
      if (address < begin) return NoSlot;
      auto offset = address - begin;
      auto id = offset>>m_shift;
      auto within = offset & (stride() - 1);
      return id < count && within < size ? unsigned(id) : NoSlot;
    }
    bool BufPool::owns(const void *packet) const { return slot(packet) != NoSlot; }
    bool BufPool::writable(const void *packet) const
    {
      auto id = slot(packet);
      return m_tx && id != NoSlot && unsigned(m_arena->txSlot(*this, id).refs) == 1;
    }
    uint8_t *BufPool::backing(unsigned id) const {
      ZmAssert_(m_arena && id < count);
      return m_arena->data() + m_offset + (uint64_t(id)<<m_shift) + m_prefix;
    }

      // A caller continuation/timer retries Pending; this never spins or waits.
      ZuUnion<int, ZeException> retry();
      void reset(); // Tx only, after both queue owners released their retired holds
      bool waiting() const { return m_socket && m_ifindex; }
      bool done() const { return m_socket && !m_ifindex; }
    
    private:
      Xsk        *m_socket = nullptr;
      unsigned    m_ifindex = 0;
      unsigned    m_queue = 0;
      Xsk        m_probe;
    };

    #include <zlib/ZxdpRetire.hh>
    
    namespace Zxdp::Xdp {
    
    KernelRetirement::~KernelRetirement() { ZmAssert_(!waiting()); }
    
    ZuUnion<int, ZeException> KernelRetirement::begin(Xsk &socket)
    {
      if (m_socket || !socket.bound())
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp",
          "kernel retirement requires a live bound socket and unused observer");
      // Same arena, no parallel payload allocation. The observer's small private
      // rings remain empty for its entire lifetime, even after a successful bind.
      auto prepared = m_probe.prepare(socket.arena(), 2, 2);
      if (prepared.is<ZeException>()) return ZuMv(prepared).p<ZeException>();
      if (m_probe.namespaceID() != socket.namespaceID()) {
        m_probe.close();
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp",
          "kernel retirement observer belongs to a different network namespace");
      }
      m_socket = &socket;
      m_ifindex = socket.ifindex();
      m_queue = socket.queue();
      socket.close();
      return retry();
    }
    
    ZuUnion<int, ZeException> KernelRetirement::retry()
    {
      if (!m_socket) return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "kernel retirement has not begun");
      if (done()) return int(Done);
      // Linux assigns pools under RTNL and refuses an occupied queue. Its deferred
      // pool release disables driver zero-copy before clearing that queue identity.
      // A successful independent bind therefore observes the old pool's retirement,
      // rather than assuming fd closure or TX cursor progress is sufficient.
      auto bound = m_probe.bind_(m_ifindex, m_queue, false);
      if (bound.is<ZeException>()) {
        if (!m_probe.retryBind()) return ZuMv(bound).p<ZeException>();
        return int(Pending);
      }
      m_probe.close(); // no FILL/TX was ever published by this observer
      m_ifindex = 0; // the observer no longer needs a target after successful bind
      return int(Done);
    }
    
    void KernelRetirement::reset()
    {
      if (!m_socket) return;
      ZmAssert_(done());
      m_socket = nullptr;
      m_ifindex = m_queue = 0;
    }

        Refactor Zxdp backends around intrusive Zi buffer pools
    
        - Rename Zi IOBufPlugin to IOBufPool and propagate the breaking pool API.
        - Select polymorphic backends with instance(Type::Xdp) and tagged parameters.
        - Isolate AF_XDP implementation and concrete buffer pools inside Zxdp::Xdp.
        - Propagate structured Ze exceptions through Zxdp and Zutcp fallible APIs.
        - Align framework usage, include groups, ownership, tests, and documentation.
        - Specify structured error contracts and the permitted use of ZeString captures.
        - Validate with Clang debug builds, unit suites, native and kernel interop tests.

    static unsigned power2(unsigned n)
    {
      if (n > (unsigned(1)<<31)) return 0;
      if (n < 2) return 2;
      return unsigned(1)<<(32 - __builtin_clz(n - 1));
    }
    
    static unsigned poolStride(const Zi::IOBufPool &pool)
    {
      unsigned size = pool.size;
      if (size < pool.align) size = pool.align;
      return power2(size < 64 ? 64 : size);
    }
    
    ZuUnion<ZmRef<UMem>, ZeException> UMem::create(
      const Zi::IOBufPoolList &txPools, Zi::IOBufPool *rxPool, unsigned mtu)
    {
      auto fail = [](const char *text) { return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", text); };
      // Linux copy-mode Rx adds NET_IP_ALIGN before the Ethernet header.
      enum { RxAlign = 2 };
      auto rx = dynamic_cast<BufPool *>(rxPool);
      auto page = sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE);
      if (page < 2048 || uint64_t(page) > UINT32_MAX || (page & (page - 1)))
        return fail("unsupported AF_XDP page size");
      if (!rx || !rx->count || rx->ready() || rx->used())
        return fail("one unused, nonempty Rx pool is required");
      if (!rx->align || (rx->align & (rx->align - 1)) || rx->align > unsigned(page) ||
          rx->headRoom > rx->size || rx->tailRoom > rx->size - rx->headRoom)
        return fail("invalid Rx pool geometry");
      unsigned prefix = rx->align > XDP_PACKET_HEADROOM ? rx->align : XDP_PACKET_HEADROOM;
      if (!mtu || rx->size < mtu + 14 || uint64_t(rx->size) + prefix + RxAlign > unsigned(page))
        return fail("Rx packet size does not fit the interface and one AF_XDP chunk");
      ArenaLayout layout;
      layout.prefix = prefix;
      layout.chunk = power2(rx->size + layout.prefix + RxAlign);
      if (layout.chunk < 2048) layout.chunk = 2048;
      layout.rxCount = rx->count;
      uint64_t txBytes = 0;
      {
        auto pools = txPools.citer();
        while (auto node = pools()) {
          auto pool = dynamic_cast<BufPool *>(node);
          if (!pool || pool == rx || pool->ready() || pool->used() || !pool->size ||
        pool->size > unsigned(page) || pool->headRoom > pool->size ||
        pool->tailRoom > pool->size - pool->headRoom || !pool->align ||
        (pool->align & (pool->align - 1)) || pool->align > unsigned(page))
        return fail("invalid or busy Tx pool");
          if (pool->count > UINT32_MAX - layout.txCount) return fail("Tx count overflow");
          layout.txCount += pool->count;
          auto stride = poolStride(*pool);
          if (stride > layout.chunk) layout.chunk = stride;
          auto bytes = uint64_t(pool->count) * stride;
          auto length = (bytes + page - 1) & ~(uint64_t(page) - 1);
          if (length > SIZE_MAX - txBytes) return fail("Tx arena size overflow");
          txBytes += length;
        }
      }
      if (layout.chunk > unsigned(page)) return fail("packet exceeds AF_XDP chunk size");
      auto rxBytes = uint64_t(rx->count) * layout.chunk;
      rxBytes = (rxBytes + page - 1) & ~(uint64_t(page) - 1);
      if (rxBytes > SIZE_MAX - txBytes) return fail("Rx arena size overflow");
      layout.rxLength = rxBytes;
      layout.txLength = txBytes;
      layout.length = rxBytes + txBytes;
      if (layout.length/layout.chunk > UINT32_MAX || layout.length/unsigned(page) > UINT32_MAX)
        return fail("AF_XDP arena exceeds kernel count limits");
      ZmRef<UMem> arena = new UMem;
      auto mem = mmap(nullptr, layout.length, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
        MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
      if (mem == MAP_FAILED) {
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", ([error = ZeLastError](auto &out) {
          out << "AF_XDP arena mmap failed: " << error;
        }));
      }
      arena->m_data = static_cast<uint8_t *>(mem);
      arena->m_layout = layout;
      arena->m_pageShift = __builtin_ctz(unsigned(page));
      arena->m_pages.length(layout.length>>arena->m_pageShift);
      arena->m_tx.length(layout.txCount);
      rx->init(arena, 0, layout.chunk, layout.prefix, 0);
      for (size_t i = 0; i < layout.rxLength>>arena->m_pageShift; ++i) arena->m_pages[i] = rx;
      uint64_t offset = rxBytes;
      unsigned first = 0;
      auto pools = txPools.citer();
      while (auto node = pools()) {
        auto pool = static_cast<BufPool *>(node);
        auto stride = poolStride(*pool);
        auto bytes = (uint64_t(pool->count) * stride + page - 1) & ~(uint64_t(page) - 1);
        pool->init(arena, offset, stride, 0, first);
        for (auto i = offset>>arena->m_pageShift; i < (offset + bytes)>>arena->m_pageShift; ++i)
          arena->m_pages[i] = pool;
        first += pool->count;
        offset += bytes;
      }
      return arena;
    }
    
    BufPool *UMem::pool(const void *packet) const
    {
      auto address = uintptr_t(packet), begin = uintptr_t(m_data);
      if (address < begin || address - begin >= m_layout.length) return nullptr;
      return m_pages[(address - begin)>>m_pageShift];
    }
    TxSlot &UMem::txSlot(const BufPool &pool, unsigned slot)
    {
      return m_tx[pool.first() + slot];
    }
    void UMem::retire(const Zi::IOBufPoolList &txPools, BufPool *rx)
    {
      rx->retire();
      auto pools = txPools.citer();
      while (auto node = pools()) static_cast<BufPool *>(node)->retire();
    }
    UMem::~UMem() { if (m_data) munmap(m_data, m_layout.length); }
    
    static ZeException socketFailed(const char *operation)
    {
      return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", ([operation, error = ZeLastError](auto &out) {
        out << operation << ": " << error;
      }));
    }
    
    template <typename R> ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Xsk::map(
      unsigned i, R &ring, const xdp_ring_offset &off, unsigned count, uint64_t offset)
    {
      size_t length;
      if (!R::mapLength(off, count, length))
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "invalid AF_XDP kernel ring offsets or mapping length");
      auto mem = mmap(nullptr, length, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, m_fd, offset);
      if (mem == MAP_FAILED) return socketFailed("AF_XDP ring mmap");
      m_maps[i] = {mem, length};
      if (!ring.init(mem, length, off, count))
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "invalid AF_XDP mapped ring state");
      return {};
    }
    
    Xsk::~Xsk() { close(); }
    
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Xsk::open(
      ZmRef<UMem> arena, unsigned ifindex, unsigned queue, unsigned rxCount, unsigned txCount,
      int shared)
    {
      auto prepared = prepare(ZuMv(arena), rxCount, txCount, shared);
      if (prepared.is<ZeException>()) return ZuMv(prepared).p<ZeException>();
      auto bound = bind(ifindex, queue);
      if (bound.is<ZeException>()) { close(); return ZuMv(bound).p<ZeException>(); }
      return {};
    }
    
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Xsk::prepare(
      ZmRef<UMem> arena, unsigned rxCount, unsigned txCount, int shared)
    {
      if (m_fd >= 0 || !arena || !rxCount || !txCount ||
          (rxCount & (rxCount - 1)) || (txCount & (txCount - 1)))
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "invalid or already open AF_XDP registration/binding");
      m_fd = socket(AF_XDP, SOCK_RAW | SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0);
      if (m_fd < 0) return socketFailed("AF_XDP socket");
      m_arena = ZuMv(arena);
      m_shared = shared;
      auto fail = [this](const char *operation) {
        auto error = socketFailed(operation);
        close();
        return error;
      };
      socklen_t namespaceLength = sizeof(m_namespace);
      if (getsockopt(m_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_NETNS_COOKIE, &m_namespace, &namespaceLength))
        return fail("AF_XDP socket namespace query");
      if (namespaceLength != sizeof(m_namespace)) {
        close();
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "AF_XDP kernel lacks socket namespace identity");
      }
      const auto &layout = m_arena->layout();
      xdp_umem_reg reg{};
      reg.addr = uintptr_t(m_arena->data());
      reg.len = layout.length;
      reg.chunk_size = layout.chunk;
      reg.headroom = layout.prefix - XDP_PACKET_HEADROOM;
      if (shared < 0 && setsockopt(m_fd, SOL_XDP, XDP_UMEM_REG, &reg, sizeof(reg)))
        return fail("AF_XDP UMEM registration");
      // Linux limits the copy-mode drain budget to Tx ring capacity. 32K permits
      // sustained concurrent publication; CQ and pool credits still bound backing.
      enum { MinTxRing = 1<<15 };
      unsigned txRingCount = txCount < MinTxRing ? MinTxRing : txCount;
      struct { unsigned option, count; } rings[] = {
        {XDP_UMEM_FILL_RING, rxCount}, {XDP_UMEM_COMPLETION_RING, txCount},
        {XDP_RX_RING, rxCount}, {XDP_TX_RING, txRingCount}
      };
      for (auto ring : rings)
        if (setsockopt(m_fd, SOL_XDP, ring.option, &ring.count, sizeof(ring.count)))
          return fail("AF_XDP ring configuration");
      // Older kernels retain their default budget when this tuning option is absent.
      if (setsockopt(m_fd, SOL_XDP, XDP_MAX_TX_SKB_BUDGET,
        &txRingCount, sizeof(txRingCount)) && errno != ENOPROTOOPT)
        return fail("AF_XDP Tx budget configuration");
      xdp_mmap_offsets offsets{};
      socklen_t length = sizeof(offsets);
      if (getsockopt(m_fd, SOL_XDP, XDP_MMAP_OFFSETS, &offsets, &length))
        return fail("AF_XDP ring offset query");
      if (length < sizeof(offsets)) {
        close();
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "AF_XDP kernel lacks required ring offset/flags ABI");
      }
      auto mapped = map(0, m_fill, offsets.fr, rxCount, XDP_UMEM_PGOFF_FILL_RING);
      if (mapped.is<void>()) mapped = map(1, m_comp, offsets.cr, txCount,
        XDP_UMEM_PGOFF_COMPLETION_RING);
      if (mapped.is<void>()) mapped = map(2, m_rx, offsets.rx, rxCount, XDP_PGOFF_RX_RING);
      if (mapped.is<void>()) mapped = map(3, m_tx, offsets.tx, txRingCount, XDP_PGOFF_TX_RING);
      if (mapped.is<ZeException>()) { close(); return ZuMv(mapped).p<ZeException>(); }
      return {};
    }
    
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Xsk::bind(unsigned ifindex, unsigned queue)
    {
      return bind_(ifindex, queue, true);
    }
    
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Xsk::bind_(unsigned ifindex, unsigned queue, bool queryOptions)
    {
      m_retryBind = false;
      if (m_fd < 0 || m_bound || !ifindex || ifindex > INT_MAX)
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "invalid or already bound AF_XDP socket");
      sockaddr_xdp address{};
      address.sxdp_family = AF_XDP;
      address.sxdp_ifindex = ifindex;
      address.sxdp_queue_id = queue;
      // Ordinary binding lets the kernel select supported zero-copy operation.
      address.sxdp_flags = XDP_USE_NEED_WAKEUP;
      if (m_shared >= 0) {
        address.sxdp_flags = XDP_SHARED_UMEM; // inherits NEED_WAKEUP from the first socket
        address.sxdp_shared_umem_fd = m_shared;
      }
      if (::bind(m_fd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr *>(&address), sizeof(address))) {
        m_retryBind = errno == EBUSY;
        return socketFailed("AF_XDP interface/queue bind");
      }
      m_bound = true;
      m_ifindex = ifindex;
      m_queue = queue;
      if (!queryOptions) return {};
      xdp_options options{};
      socklen_t length = sizeof(options);
      if (getsockopt(m_fd, SOL_XDP, XDP_OPTIONS, &options, &length)) {
        auto error = socketFailed("AF_XDP capability query");
        close();
        return error;
      }
      if (length < sizeof(options)) {
        close();
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zxdp", "AF_XDP kernel lacks capability flags");
      }
      m_zeroCopy = options.flags & XDP_OPTIONS_ZEROCOPY;
      return {};
    }
    
    void Xsk::close()
    {
      m_rx.freeze(); m_fill.freeze(); m_tx.freeze(); m_comp.freeze();
      if (m_fd >= 0) { ::close(m_fd); m_fd = -1; }
      m_rx.reset();
      m_fill.reset();
      m_tx.reset();
      m_comp.reset();
      for (unsigned i = 4; i; --i) {
        auto &mapping = m_maps[i - 1];
        if (mapping.addr) munmap(mapping.addr, mapping.length);
        mapping = {};
      }
      m_zeroCopy = false;
      m_bound = m_retryBind = false;
      m_ifindex = m_queue = 0;
      m_namespace = 0;
      m_shared = -1;
      m_arena = nullptr;
    }
    
    } // namespace Zxdp::Xdp

    # Z framework engineering principles
    
    Part of the repository guidance mapped in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).
    Read before code changes; consult the map for task-specific rules.
    
    **Act as a principal software engineer who is a leading global expert
    in performance-oriented low-latency C++ systems and network programming.**
    
    ## Target systems
    - compilers: current gcc, clang
    - CPU: x64 intel/amd, ARM
    - OS: linux, windows
    
    ## General principles
    - time-to-market / engineering velocity is less important than:
      - design/implementation integrity
      - run-time performance
    - latency is more important than throughput
    - copying and heap memory allocations are minimized
      - where heap allocations are necessary, they use tunable heaps, except for
        objects managed by `ZmSingleton` or `ZmSpecific`
    - dependent compatibility is a non-goal unless otherwise directed
      - propagate breaking API changes to dependent code
      - do not use shims, forwarders or other such techniques for legacy compatibility purposes
    - software must be capable of running 24x7 indefinitely without process kill
      - prohibit monotonically growing memory consumption
      - all long-lived containers must be actively garbage collected
    - shutdown/teardown must be graceful and clean of leaks
    - no background garbage collection or scanning for GC
      - garbage collection must be deterministic, timely and not timer-based
    - intrusive reference counting and container nodes
    - sharding:
      - controlled thread creation
      - threads dedicated to specific work and thread-affined data
      - fast inter-thread communication with ring buffers
    - asynchronous continuation-based functional style
    
    ### No dogma
    - immutability
      - pervasive immutability is a non-goal
      - mutability is encouraged if it benefits performance
        - example: in-place encrypt plaintext, decrypt ciphertext for TLS
        - example: in-place decoding of strings in JSON parsing
    - type punning and undefined behavior
      - avoiding UB that is purely theoretical or limited to non-targeted systems is a non-goal
      - UB type punning is endorsed unless it actually creates a **tangible correctness or security risk** for targeted systems
    - not header-only
      - **intentionally** not header-only
      - Z libraries are traditional hybrid builds
        - headers with accompanying binary versioned shared libraries / DLLs
    - intrusive + intrinsic
      - non-intrusive or extrinsic storage is a non-goal (no STL containers)
    - sentinel values
      - sentinel values for logical null or false, not extrinsic booleans
    - Postel's Law, unabashedly
      - “Be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept.”
      - conformance policing is a non-goal
      - elide all excessive correctness and validation in favor of performance
      - this principle applied to all protocols and formats for maximum resilience

        ## Analysis and adopted design
        
        ### Backend selection and instance parameters
        
        Extend the existing declarations in `Zxdp.hh` using its current enum macro form:
        
        ```cpp

        ZtEnumNS(ZxdpAPI, Type, uint8_t, Xdp, Dpdk);
        
        // Existing Params_ retains its owning Tx list, Rx reference, callback,
        // spin, scheduler and txStopped fields.
        namespace Dpdk {
          struct Params : public Params_ {
            ZtString<> name;            // DPDK Ethernet device name
            unsigned rxInterval = 50;   // maximum idle wait, microseconds; zero polls
          };
        }
        ZuDerive(Params, (ZuUnion<Xdp::Params, Dpdk::Params>));
        
        } // namespace Zxdp
        ```
        
        Use `instance(Type::Dpdk)` to obtain `Dpdk::Instance`, then allocate pools,
        populate backend parameters in place, and call `init(config)`. For example:
        
        ```cpp

        auto &params = config.p<Zxdp::Dpdk::Params>();
        params.name = "net_ring0";
        params.txPools.pushNode(tx.ptr());
        params.rxPool = rx;
        params.rx = receive;

        params.rxInterval = 50;

        the parameter union may expire after init. Retain pool references for packets

        received by DPDK send already identifies its mbuf; submit it directly without
        payload copies or external-buffer attachment. True means accepted submission;

        ### Receive idle policy
        
        The adopted priority order is sustained receive latency, avoiding extended full
        CPU consumption, then packet-triggered wake from extended idle.
        
        1. While packets arrive, immediately retrieve the next burst. Check counted wake
           state between bounded batches. No sleep or wait syscall on sustained input.
        2. After empty input, spin for `Params_::spin` rounds; any packet resets the

        3. Use native packet-arrival waiting where available. Ring producer-head memory

    ---
    name: egm-review-loop
    license: Apache-2.0
    disable-model-invocation: true
    description: >-
      Executes the Antagonistic-Review process from the Elephant-Goldfish
      Model (EGM) via an automated multi-agent review loop to audit documents
      against qualitative standards and structural templates, and automatically
      apply approved fixes. Use when reviewing design docs, READMEs, feature

    ---
    
    # Goldfish Review: Loop (Orchestration Driver)
    
    When running in Codex or ChatGPT Work, first read [Codex integration](../../docs/codex.md).
    In Claude Code or Cowork, read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/docs/claude.md` first.
    
    ## Overview
    
    This skill acts as the central orchestration engine driving the multi-agent
    review loop. It coordinates two distinct agent memory models:
    
    *   **The Goldfish (Adversarial Auditors)**: Subagents spawned in isolated,
        fresh context windows to catch unstated assumptions without historical bias.
    *   **The Elephant (Persistent Resolver)**: The primary agent context holding
        institutional knowledge to evaluate findings and apply approved repairs.
    
    The driver manages argument intake, resolves paths for reviewers and standards,
    unconditionally re-parses target line ranges before every iteration, spawns
    concurrent specialized Goldfish auditors based on configuration, and coordinates
    with the Elephant context to resolve findings.
    
    ## Delegation
    
    A Goldfish runs in a fresh context with no conversation history. Spawn each
    subagent with your harness's subagent tool (Antigravity: `invoke_subagent`; Claude Code: `Agent`; Codex: `spawn_agent`). Each subagent is defined in `agents/<file>.md`, and its
    frontmatter `name` (for example `egm-zoom-out`) is the subagent type to request
    where your harness registers named subagents. Otherwise spawn a general-purpose
    subagent and tell it to read that persona file first. Pass the prompt verbatim
    and wait for the report. If your harness cannot nest subagents,
    use direct dispatch instead of the synthesizer. See `docs/harnesses.md`.
    If your harness has no subagent tool, stop and tell the user: a review in the same
    context is not a Goldfish review.
    
    ## Inputs
    
    The caller or user provides exactly these parameters:
    
    *   **`TargetFile`**: Absolute or relative path to target document.
    *   **`SemanticTarget`**: Descriptive targeting string (e.g., *"Target the H4
        block with SS-ID 'S1.12'"*), or `full file`.
    *   **`Reviewers`**: List of reviewer names (shortnames or paths).
    *   **`Standards`**: Mapping of reviewer names to standard names (shortnames or
        paths).
    *   **`GoldfishContext`**: A reading list (source files, directories, or
        documentation URLs) fed to reviewers to establish their baseline. An empty
        list from the caller counts as provided; do not ask for it again. Some
        reviewers cannot open URLs, so before the first round save the raw page of
        each URL as a new file in the working directory (or your harness's artifact
        directory) and pass its absolute path instead. If a page cannot be saved,
        ask the user for a local copy and end your turn; if no one can answer,
        as in a headless run, leave it out, tell the user, and keep going.
    
    ## Path & Standard Resolution Logic
    
    When resolving names in `Reviewers` and `Standards`:
    
    *   **Reviewer Shortnames**: Map reviewer shortname (e.g., `design_critic`,
        `structural`, `style`, `implementation_readiness`,
        `codebase_details`, `comprehension`, `zoom_out`) to `agents/{name}.md`.
        The persona file defines the reviewer's core mandates, audit vectors, and
        output format.
    *   **Standard Shortnames**: Map standard shortname (e.g., `feature-spec-standard`,
        `implementation-readiness-standard`, `zoom-out-standard`, `heilmeier-standard`,
        `re-implementation-standard`) to `resources/document_standards/{name}.md`.
    *   **Custom Paths**: If the name contains a slash (`/`), treat it as an
        absolute or workspace-relative path and read it directly.
    
    ## Execution Workflow
    
    ### Step 1: Intake & Configuration UX
    
    Evaluate the provided inputs (`TargetFile`, `SemanticTarget`, `Reviewers`,
    `Standards`, `GoldfishContext`).
    
    1.  **Identify Missing Inputs**: Determine which of the required parameters are
        missing.
    2.  **Interactive Onboarding**:
        *   If **all** inputs are present, proceed to Step 2.
        *   If **some or all** inputs are missing, interactively prompt the user
            **only for the missing inputs**, one at a time via chat messages.
    3.  **Reviewer Recommendations**:
        *   *Feature Specs*: Recommend `design_critic` (mapped to
            `resources/document_standards/feature-spec-standard.md`) and
            `structural` (mapped to `resources/document_standards/feature-spec-standard.md`).
        *   *Implementation Plans*: Recommend `implementation_readiness`
            (mapped to `resources/document_standards/implementation-readiness-standard.md`)
            and `codebase_details`.
    4.  **Confirm Configuration**: Display the consolidated plan (Target, Reviewers,
        and mapped Standards) and ask the user to confirm before proceeding.
    
    ### Step 2: The Sharpening Loop (Iterative Cycle)
    
    Execute the following sequence in a continuous loop:
    
    #### 2.1 Unconditional Target Resolution
    
    Before every iteration, unconditionally re-scan `TargetFile` by reading it
    and using the stable `SemanticTarget` string (e.g., locating the target header) to
    dynamically determine the updated absolute start and end line numbers. This
    ensures absolute accuracy even if the file was edited in prior rounds. (If `full
    file` mode is specified, confirm full-file line bounds).
    
    #### 2.2 Review Swarm Execution
    
    1.  **Launch Subagent Swarm**:
        Spawn subagents to execute the review:
        *   **Hierarchical Dispatch (Synthesizer)**: Spawn the intermediate
            synthesizer subagent (`agents/synthesizer.md` / `egm-synthesizer`).
            The synthesizer spawns the Goldfish review swarm in
            parallel, deduplicates findings, writes the report artifact, and
            returns a single summary message to avoid context pollution in the root
            conversation. Pass it the Failed Reviewers rule below and
            `GoldfishContext`, and tell it to give those files to each reviewer.
            Its summary must give a status, `completed` or `not run`, for each
            requested reviewer.
        *   **Direct Dispatch (Flat Swarm)**: Alternatively, spawn each requested
            reviewer subagent in `Reviewers` directly.
            Instruct each subagent to first read its persona definition in
            `agents/{name}.md`, then audit `TargetFile` at the resolved line range
            against its designated standard in `resources/document_standards/`,
            supplying `GoldfishContext`.
        *   Each reviewer produces findings with severity (🔴 Blocker, 🟡 Major, 🟢
            Nit), line numbers, discrepancy descriptions, and rationales.
    2.  **Consolidate Findings**: Collect all findings across reviewers into a single
        flat `FindingsList`. Give each finding a stable id
        (`<reviewer>-<round>-<n>`) and record its reviewer, severity, and affected
        scope.
    3.  **Failed Reviewers**: A reviewer that times out, fails, or returns no report
        did not review. Retry it once. If it fails again, record it as **not run**
        in the report. Never count it as a reviewer with zero findings. If the
        synthesizer summary has no status for a requested reviewer, record that
        reviewer as not run.
    
    #### 2.3 Aggregated Resolution Hand-off
    
    1.  Pass `TargetFile`, the active line range, and the aggregated `FindingsList`
        to the **`egm-resolve`** workflow.
    2.  Execute the resolution workflow in the primary Elephant context:
        *   Categorize findings into `CONTEST` vs. `PROPOSE FIX`.
        *   Save `goldfish_review_report.md` with your file-writing tool.
        *   Present the interactive decision gate (Auto accept, Continue, Interactive
            breakdown).
        *   Apply approved text repairs to `TargetFile` using your file-editing tool.
    
    #### 2.4 Iteration Check & Turn Boundary
    
    Fresh reviewers sample differently each round, so a round with zero findings
    is rare even when the document improves. Use these rules instead:
    
    *   **Settled findings**: A finding is settled when it is contested or
        recorded without a fix (accepted risk). Keep the settled list across
        rounds. If a new reviewer raises a settled finding again (same affected
        scope, same issue), do not re-open it.
    *   **Fixed findings**: An applied fix does not settle a finding. If a later
        reviewer raises the same issue at the same scope, the fix failed or a
        later edit reintroduced the issue. Re-open the finding.
    *   **Clean round**: A round is clean when no reviewer raises a Blocker or
        Major finding that is not settled. Nits do not block. A reviewer recorded
        as not run makes the round not clean. Decide this from the review results,
        before you apply the fixes of that round.
    *   **Converged**: Two consecutive clean rounds. One clean round is not enough,
        because the next fresh reviewer can find a different gap in the same text.
    *   **Cap**: 5 rounds.
    *   **Churn**: A new finding is at the scope of an applied fix, and reverting
        that fix would resolve it.
    
    On converged, go to Step 3. On cap or churn, write a short list of the open
    findings by severity, then ask the user one question: accept and proceed,
    continue past the cap, or return the document to drafting.
    
    **Crucial Turn-Taking Requirement**: After the resolution phase finishes for a
    given round, the loop driver **MUST respect the turn-taking checkpoint in
    `egm-resolve`**. The driver must remain idle across human turns,
    only looping back to Step 2.1 when the user explicitly confirms they wish to run
    another round of review.
    
    ### Step 3: Output Boundary & Final Checkpoint
    
    Upon completion (converged, cap or churn accepted by the user, or manual
    halt):
    
    *   **Programmatic Callers**: If running as a subflow of `egm-review`, exit

    *   **Manual Invocations**: Output a summary of completion in chat: *"The review
        loop has completed after [N] rounds ([converged | accepted at cap | halted]).
    Open findings are in the report. Would you like to proceed to
        the next stage, or do you have any final questions?"*

    # Instructions
    
    Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller:
    
    ### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)

    2. **Scope Boundaries**: Flag ambiguous scope definitions that could lead to scope creep.
    3. Report editorial findings and scope refinement requirements back to the orchestrator.

    2. **Verify Objectivity & Claim Calibration**: Ensure all claims are factual, measurable, and verifiable. Flag subjective evaluations of code quality or system performance, require every caveat to name a concrete reader/operator decision, and require every claim about existing or tested behavior to match its evidence.
    3. **Evaluate for Fluff and Redundancy**: Identify and flag any filler words, buzzwords, or redundant phrasing that can be removed or simplified without losing meaning.
    4. **Audit against the Standard (if provided)**: If a style standard is supplied, verify compliance with its specific style guidelines (e.g., active voice requirements, terminology constraints).
    
    ### Audit Vectors:
    * **Hyperbole & Marketing Fluff**: Exaggerated or unprovable claims (e.g., "flawless execution," "revolutionary design," "fully eliminates all bugs").
    * **Jargon & Buzzwords**: Non-precise terms that obscure meaning (e.g., "leverage the framework," "synergistic integration").
    * **Filler Words & Wordiness**: Phrases that add noise instead of signal (e.g., "essentially," "simply run the command," "it is important to note that").
    * **Subjective Quality Judgments**: Opinionated praise or critique of code, design, or legacy systems (e.g., "beautifully structured class," "terrible legacy parser").
    * **Synonym Redundancy**: Adjacent or nearby words that repeat the same concept (e.g., "quick and rapid," "clean and elegant").
    * **Defensive Caveats & Uncalibrated Claims (`DROP | CALIBRATE | RELOCATE | KEEP`)**: Blanket disclaimers for inactive failure modes, speculative hedging with no reachable operator decision, or capability claims about existing or tested behavior that outrun actual verification evidence. Classify each flagged sentence as `DROP` (no concrete reader decision), `CALIBRATE` (narrow claim to verified scope/evidence), `RELOCATE` (move operational caveat to the exact step where a user makes a choice), or `KEEP` (backed by concrete evidence; do not report it as a finding).

    # Implementation Readiness Standard
    
    This standard defines the quality bar for implementation plans and task lists.
    
    ## Core Principle
    
    A plan passes if a competent engineer (or fresh AI session) who is unfamiliar
    with the codebase can execute the plan and produce the correct changes on the
    first attempt, without guessing, asking clarifying questions, or making
    independent design choices.
    
    ## The Zero-Decision Rule
    
    The plan must leave **zero design or architectural choices to the implementer**.
    If the implementer must make design choices (including, but not limited to,
    choosing a database schema, designing an API path, selecting a dependency, or
    deciding how to handle a new edge case), the plan **fails** this standard. All
    such decisions must be pre-determined and documented in the plan.
    
    ## Phasing & Checkpoints
    
    The plan must partition the work into logical, incremental phases. Each phase
    must leave the codebase in a stable, buildable, and testable state.
    
    ## Requirements (Non-Exhaustive Examples)
    
    The plan must detail these areas if applicable to the proposed changes:
    
    *   **Target Scope & File Boundary**: Explicit list of exact repository-relative
        file paths to be created, modified, or deleted, suitable for enforcing a
        Phase 5 write allowlist without unapproved adjacent refactors or
        opportunistic dependency additions. Use a directory glob only for generated
        output whose filenames can't be known in advance.
    *   **Actionable Steps**: Precise logic changes, data transformations, and API
        updates for each file.
    *   **Test Plan**: Specific test cases (happy path and edge cases) that must be
        implemented.

    ---
    name: egm-resolve
    license: Apache-2.0
    disable-model-invocation: true
    description: >-
      The Elephant resolution skill. Ingests flat deficiency reports from
      concurrent Goldfish reviewers, applies automated fixes for PROPOSE FIX
      items via UI multiple-choice gates, and presents interactive
      negotiation/re-sync checkpoints.
    ---
    
    # Goldfish Review: Resolve
    
    When running in Codex or ChatGPT Work, first read [Codex integration](../../docs/codex.md).
    In Claude Code or Cowork, read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/docs/claude.md` first.
    
    ## Overview
    
    This skill instructs the agent on how to operate within the primary Elephant
    context window to parse flat deficiency reports from concurrent Goldfish
    reviewers. It defends accurate design choices, applies automated textual
    repairs, and manages interactive negotiation checkpoints.
    
    ## Prerequisites & Context Strategy
    
    *   **Context Recommendation (Elephant Memory)**: This skill should be run in
        the persistent conversation session that generated the target document (the
        Elephant) to recall earlier reasoning and craft higher-quality fixes.
    
    ## Inputs
    
    The caller or orchestration driver provides exactly these parameters:
    
    *   **`TargetFile`**: Absolute or relative path to target document.
    *   **`LineRange`**: Exact line numbers (or `full file`).
    *   **`FindingsList`**: Aggregated flat list of findings from Goldfish
        reviewers.
    
    ## Execution Workflow
    
    ### Step 1: Intake Validation & Gather Context
    
    1.  **Hybrid Execution UX**: Detect if execution arguments are present:
    
        *   *Automated Mode*: If all parameters are provided, execute silently as a
            subprocess.
        *   *Standalone Human Mode*: If parameters are omitted, trigger a friendly
            onboarding flow. Prompt for one piece of input at a time, waiting for
            the user's response after each turn. Once all inputs are specified,
            display the final setup and verify the user is ready to continue.
    
    2.  Read `TargetFile` at `LineRange` by reading it and parse the `FindingsList`.
    
    ### Step 2: Evaluate & Categorize
    
    Give each finding exactly one category:
    
    *   **CONTEST**: The critique is inaccurate or relies on a misunderstanding of
        the codebase. Cite evidence that the reviewer could read: a file and
        symbol, or a decision recorded in the document.
    *   **ESCALATE**: The critique is inaccurate, but the evidence is outside every
        file the reviewer could read (for example, a team convention or a verbal
        decision). State that fact. Do not fix the finding. Give it to the user.
    *   **PROPOSE FIX**: The critique is valid. Define precise textual replacements
        or structural formatting adjustments to resolve the gap.
    *   **DECLINE**: The finding is a Nit. Record it. Do not fix it. You can use
        PROPOSE FIX for a Nit if the fix is worth it.
    
    Apply these rules:
    
    *   **A contest must be checkable.** "This was intentional" is not evidence.
        If you cannot cite evidence the reviewer could read, use ESCALATE or
        PROPOSE FIX.
    *   **Do not add context only to satisfy a reviewer.** Add context when a human
        reader of the document needs it. If only a zero-context subagent needs it,
        use ESCALATE.
    *   **Do not contest a comprehension gap.** If a fresh reader could not follow
        the document, the document is missing context.
    *   **Do not change a severity.** If you think a Blocker is a Nit, CONTEST it
        and state the reason.
    *   You wrote the document under review. A wish to contest is not evidence
        that the reviewer is wrong.
    
    ### Step 3: Report Fixes
    
    Construct the final report and save it named
    `goldfish_review_report.md` in the working directory (or your harness's artifact directory, if it has one)
    using your file-writing tool. Use this layout:
    
    ```markdown
    # Goldfish Annotated Review Report
    
    **Target:** `[TargetFile]` (`[LineRange]`)
    
    ## Prioritized Findings & AI Suggestions
    
    {{range findings, ordered by Severity}}
    ### [Issue 1] [`[ReviewerPersona]`] - Severity: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
    *   **Affected Scope:** [Lines Start-End]([RelativePath]#L[Start]-L[End]) ([Sub-header])
    *   **Discrepancy Description:** [copied from FindingsList]
    *   **Rationale:** [copied from FindingsList]
    *   ***AI Suggestion:*** [CONTEST | ESCALATE | PROPOSE FIX | DECLINE]
    *   ***Justification:*** [Detailed reason]
    *   ***Proposed Edit:***
        *   Location: [Line/Header]
        *   Change: [Precise replacement string or deletion note]
    {{end}}
    ```
    
    ### Step 4: Interactive Resolution Gate
    
    If any finding is `ESCALATE`, list those findings first in the chat message.
    They need the user's knowledge, not only approval.
    
    Before proceeding, output a visible chat message to the user: *"I have compiled
    the audit findings into `goldfish_review_report.md`. Please review the findings there and choose how you would like to
    proceed:
    
    -   **Comment directly on the file**: Review `goldfish_review_report.md` in
        chat or the file and leave comments/edits to approve, reject, or contest
        specific items.
    -   **Auto accept**: Reply "auto accept" to batch-apply all proposed fixes
        (skipping contested items).
    -   **Continue to next phase**: Reply "continue" or "no changes" to proceed
        without applying fixes.
    -   **Interactive breakdown**: Reply "interactive breakdown" for a guided,
        item-by-item walkthrough in chat with detailed explanations for each
        proposed edit or contested finding before making decisions.
    -   **Custom instruction / Wildcard request**: Reply with any custom
        instruction, question, or out-of-band request."*
    
    You **MUST** immediately yield active execution by calling **zero tools** in
    this turn payload. You must stop execution and go idle, waiting for the human
    developer to comment on/edit the artifact or reply in the chat.
    
    Interpret the user's action/response as follows:
    
    -   **"Auto accept" / "Accept all suggestions" / User clicks "Proceed" without
        contesting**: Apply all fixes where the AI suggestion was `PROPOSE FIX`
        directly to `TargetFile` at `LineRange` in a single batch using
        your file-editing tool. Any items categorized as `CONTEST`, `ESCALATE`, or
        `DECLINE` are explicitly bypassed. Then proceed to Step 5.
    -   **"Continue to next phase" / "No changes"**: Do not apply any automated
        fixes. Then proceed to Step 5.
    -   **"Interactive breakdown"**: Enter a sequential breakdown loop over ALL
        finding items (all categories except `DECLINE`):
    
        1.  For each item `i`, output a visible chat message formatting the full
            finding details and explanation in rich markdown:
    
            ```markdown
            ### Breakdown Item [i]: [Issue Title] [`[ReviewerPersona]`]
            * **Scope:** [Lines Start-End]([RelativePath]#L[Start]-L[End]) ([Sub-header])
            * **Description:** [Description]
            * **AI Suggestion:** [CONTEST | ESCALATE | PROPOSE FIX]
            * **Explanation & Justification:** [Detailed reason and background explaining why the fix is proposed or why the finding is contested]
            * **Proposed Edit:** [Precise replacement text or deletion note]
            ```
    
            Then prompt the user in chat for their decision on this item (calling
            **zero tools** and going idle):
    
            *   If `PROPOSE FIX`: Ask the user to reply with **Accept proposed
                fix**, **Skip / ignore**, or **Discuss**.
            *   If `CONTEST`: Ask the user to reply with **Skip / agree with
                contest**, **Overrule contest (propose fix)**, or **Discuss**.
            *   If `ESCALATE`: Ask the user to reply with **Confirm (no change)**,
                **Add the fact to the document**, or **Discuss**.
    
        2.  Record the user's decisions in an internal memory checklist (e.g., *Item
            1: Accepted*, *Item 2: Ignored*, *Item 3: Overruled*). **Do NOT call any
            file editing tools during this sequential loop.**
    
        3.  Once all items have been decided, summarize the accepted edits, execute
            them using your file-editing tool, and proceed to Step 5.
    
    -   **Custom instruction / Out-of-band edit**: If the user provides targeted
        instructions, apply them and proceed.
    
    ### Step 5: Post-Resolution Synchronization & Exit
    
    1.  **Re-verify Lines**: If changes were made to `TargetFile`, verify that the
        file remains structurally coherent and valid markdown.
    2.  Mark the report as resolved (add a `Status: resolved` line at the top).
    3.  **Handoff**: Exit cleanly back to the caller (such as `egm-review-loop`)
        with the count of accepted fixes, contested items, escalated items,
        declined items, and remaining unaddressed issues.

    13218:The rte_eth_tx_burst() function is invoked to transmit output packets on the output queue queue_id of the Ethernet device designated by its port_id. The nb_pkts parameter is the number of packets to send which are supplied in the tx_pkts array of rte_mbuf structures, each of them allocated from a pool created with rte_pktmbuf_pool_create(). The rte_eth_tx_burst() function loops, sending nb_pkts packets, up to the number of transmit descriptors available in the Tx ring of the transmit queue. For each packet to send, the rte_eth_tx_burst() function performs the following operations:
    13226:In the case of a segmented packet composed of a list of rte_mbuf buffers, the rte_eth_tx_burst() function uses several transmit descriptors of the ring.
    13228:The rte_eth_tx_burst() function returns the number of packets it actually sent. A return value equal to nb_pkts means that all packets have been sent, and this is likely to signify that other output packets could be immediately transmitted again. Applications that implement a "send as many packets to transmit as possible" policy can check this specific case and keep invoking the rte_eth_tx_burst() function until a value less than nb_pkts is returned.

    Request the driver to free mbufs currently cached by the driver. The driver will only free the mbuf if it is no longer in use. It is the application's responsibility to ensure rte_eth_tx_buffer_flush(..) is called if needed.
    
    Parameters
    
    
    port_idThe port identifier of the Ethernet device.
    
    
    queue_idThe index of the transmit queue through which output packets must be sent. The value must be in the range [0, nb_tx_queue - 1] previously supplied to rte_eth_dev_configure().
    
    
    free_cntMaximum number of packets to free. Use 0 to indicate all possible packets should be freed. Note that a packet may be using multiple mbufs.
    
    
    
    ReturnsFailure: < 0 -ENODEV: Invalid interface -EIO: device is removed -ENOTSUP: Driver does not support function Success: >= 0 0-n: Number of packets freed. More packets may still remain in ring that are in use.

## User

"derives pool geometry from a Linux interface" - explain that

## Assistant

Zutcp currently queries the Linux interface’s **MTU before allocating its packet pools**:

- [`requireMTU()`](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpMx.cc:646) calls `interfaceMTU(interface)`.
- The [Stack constructor](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpMx.cc:669) stores that result as `m_mtu`.
- It creates Rx and Tx pools with buffer size `m_mtu + 14`, allowing for the Ethernet header. Tx pools also reserve protocol headroom.

So “geometry” was broader than necessary: the specific dependency is **buffer size derived from the Linux interface MTU**. Pool counts come from other configuration.

For DPDK, this sizing should obtain the MTU from the selected DPDK port instead. The pool factory already provides the backend-specific allocation boundary.

## User

why does `Zxdp::Instance` provide `mtu` if MTU is an input to it via the pools?

## Assistant

The pool specifies **buffer capacity**, while `Instance::mtu()` reports the device’s configured MTU. They need not be equal—for example, a 2048-byte buffer can serve a device with a 1500-byte MTU.

Currently, AF_XDP initialization queries the interface MTU and checks that the supplied pools can accommodate its frames. The pools do not configure the interface MTU.

The awkward part is initialization order: Zutcp queries MTU before creating pools, then Zxdp queries it again during `init()`. The accessor currently exposes the latter result only after initialization. That duplicates device discovery; it does not make pool size the MTU input.

So why is `zutcp` querying MTU to set the size?

    Stack::~Stack()
    {
      ZmAssert_(m_state == Stopped && !m_current && !unsigned(m_wakeUsers));
      ZmAssert_(m_waitProviders.empty_() && !m_allocDraining);
      ZmAssert_(!m_txServicing && !m_txPending &&
        !m_ingress->pool->used() && !m_packets->pool->used());
      ZmAssert_(!m_control->pool->used());
      ZmAssert_(!m_routePending && !m_endpoints->count_());
      ZmAssert_(!m_observed && !m_observedCount);
      delete m_cxns;
      m_ingress->rxFrames->reconcile();
      m_ingress->returned = {};
      m_backend = nullptr;
      while (m_providers) {
        auto p = m_providers;
        m_providers = p->nextProvider;
        p->nextProvider = nullptr;
        ZmAssert_(!p->pool->used() && p->waits.empty_() && !unsigned(p->notify));
        p->stack = nullptr;
        ZmDEREF(p); // stopped, long-lived configuration ownership
      }
    }
    
    void Stack::addProvider(Allocator *p)
    {
      p->queueID = ZuID{} << "allocation-waits:" << ZuBoxPtr(p).hex<false>();
      p->waits.queueOwner(mx()->id());
      p->waits.queueName(p->queueID);
      ZmREF(p);
      m_txCapacity += p->pool->count;
      p->nextProvider = m_providers;
      m_providers = p;
    }
    
    Zi::IOBufPool *Stack::allocator(
      Zi::IOBufType::T type, unsigned size, unsigned align, unsigned count)
    {
      ZmAssert_(mx()->state() == ZmEngineState::Stopped);
      // Providers reserve complete output framing before Zi copies their geometry.
      enum { Ethernet = 14, IPv6 = 40, TCP = 60 };
      unsigned head;
      switch (type) {
        case Zi::IOBufType::RxTCP:
        case Zi::IOBufType::TxTCP: head = Ethernet + IPv6 + TCP; break;
        default: throw ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zutcp", "unsupported network allocator role");
      }
      if (head >= m_mtu + Ethernet || !align || (align & (align - 1)) ||
          align > unsigned(sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)))
        throw ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zutcp", "unsupported packet allocator geometry");
      if (type == Zi::IOBufType::RxTCP)
        return new RxAllocator{m_ingress, head, count, align};
      uint64_t bytes = uint64_t(size) + head;
      if (bytes > m_mtu + Ethernet) bytes = m_mtu + Ethernet;
      auto p = new Allocator{m_backend->bufPool(count, unsigned(bytes), head, 0, align)};
      p->stack = this;
      addProvider(p);
      return p;
    }
    
    ZuUnion<void, ZeException> Stack::configureControl(unsigned count, unsigned credits)
    {
      ZmAssert_(mx()->state() == ZmEngineState::Stopped && m_state == Stopped);
      uint64_t capacity = m_txCapacity - m_control->pool->count + count;
      if (!count || !credits || credits >= capacity || capacity > UINT_MAX ||
          m_txPending || m_control->pool->used()) {
        return ZeEXCEPT(Error, "Zutcp", ([count, credits, capacity,
          held = m_control->pool->used()](auto &out) {
          out << "invalid or busy control reserve count=" << count
        << " credits=" << credits << " Tx capacity=" << capacity
        << " held control=" << held;
        }));
      }
      m_control->count = m_control->pool->count = count;
      m_controlCredits = credits;
      m_txCapacity = capacity;
      return {};
    }
    
    TxAdmission Stack::txAdmission() const
    {
      ZmAssert_(m_state == Stopped || mx()->invoked(mx()->txThread()));
      unsigned count = m_control->pool->count, used = m_control->pool->used();
      return {.capacity = m_txCapacity, .dataStalls = m_dataStalls,
        .controlStalls = m_controlStalls, .reserved = m_controlCredits,
        .outstanding = m_txPending, .controlCount = count,
        .controlFree = used < count ? count - used : 0};
    }

## Assistant

Zutcp queries MTU to **cap transport-buffer capacity**, not to replace the application’s requested size. Its allocator currently computes:

```cpp
bytes = min(requestedSize + protocolHeadroom, mtu + ethernetHeader);
```

That happens in [`Stack::allocator()`](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpMx.cc:738). The MTU-sized pools in its constructor are separate internal pools. My earlier explanation conflated them with application-requested pools.

Tracing Zdb reveals a more substantial mismatch with your intended path:

- Zdb requests table-specific buffers as [`IOBufType::App`](/home/count0/src/z/zdb/src/ZdbBuf.hh:179).
- [`ZiMultiplex::allocator()`](/home/count0/src/z/zi/src/ZiMultiplex.hh:1031) delegates to the plugin only for Rx/Tx TCP/UDP types.
- Consequently, those Zdb `App` allocations currently bypass Zutcp’s pool provider and use the builtin allocator.

So the MTU query has a purpose—constraining transport allocations—but **the current code does not provide the end-to-end application allocation path you describe**. The integration plan needs to address that boundary, rather than merely substitute a DPDK MTU query for the Linux one.

## User

Zdb should request `TxTCP` buffers

## Assistant

I’ll add that to the integration plan: Zdb’s table replication allocator will request `TxTCP` buffers through `ZiMultiplex::allocator()`.

    namespace Zutcp {
    
    RxAccount::~RxAccount() { ZmAssert_(!frames); }
    
    RxFrames::RxFrames(unsigned count, unsigned limit) : m_limit{limit}
    {
      ZmAssert_(count && limit && limit <= count);
      m_slots.length(count);
    }
    
    RxFrames::~RxFrames()
    {
      ZmAssert_(!m_retained && unsigned(m_returns) == NoSlot);
    }
    
    bool RxFrames::retain(unsigned id, RxAccount *account)
    {
      reconcile();
      ZmAssert_(id < m_slots.length() && account);
      auto &slot = m_slots[id];
      if (slot.account) {
        if (slot.account == account) return true; // aliases charge once
        ++m_refused;
        return false;
      }
      if (m_retained >= m_limit || account->frames >= account->limit) {
        ++m_refused;
        return false;
      }
      slot.account = account;
      ++account->frames;
      ++m_retained;
      ++m_admitted;
      return true;
    }
    
    void RxFrames::returned(unsigned id)
    {
      ZmAssert_(id < m_slots.length());
      auto &slot = m_slots[id];
      unsigned head;
      do {
        head = m_returns;
        slot.next = head;
      } while (m_returns.cmpXch(id, head) != head);
    }
    
    unsigned RxFrames::reconcile()
    {
      // Final return publishes here before making the physical slot reusable.
      // An empty acquire avoids exchanging a cache line on every ingress probe.
      if (unsigned(m_returns) == NoSlot) return 0;
      unsigned retired = 0;
      auto id = m_returns.xch(NoSlot);
      while (id != NoSlot) {
        auto &slot = m_slots[id];
        auto next = slot.next;
        if (slot.account) {
          ZmAssert_(slot.account->frames && m_retained);
          --slot.account->frames;
          --m_retained;
          slot.account = nullptr;
          ++retired;
        }
        id = next;
      }
      m_retired += retired;
      return retired;
    }
    
    RxFrameStats RxFrames::stats() const
    {
      return {m_admitted, m_refused, m_retired, unsigned(m_slots.length()),
        m_limit, m_retained};
    }
    
    void RxFrames::limit(unsigned value)
    {
      ZmAssert_(value && value <= m_slots.length());
      reconcile();
      m_limit = value;
    }
    
    Allocator::~Allocator()
    {
      ZmAssert_(waits.empty_() && !unsigned(notify));
    }
    
    uint8_t *Allocator::alloc()
    {
      // Once queued, producers receive reserved grants in FIFO order. An already
      // racing allocation may finish, but fresh traffic cannot starve the queue.
      if (ZuUnlikely(unsigned(notify) & Waiting)) return nullptr;
      return pool->alloc();
    }
    void Allocator::free(uint8_t *packet)
    {
      // Publish before raw free makes this slot eligible for FILL again. Rx must
      // reconcile before dispatching its next incarnation. No account is touched
      // by an off-owner producer and no access to packet bytes follows raw free.
      if (rxFrames) rxFrames->returned(pool->slot(packet));
      pool->free(packet);
      if (returned) returned();
      notifyReturn();
    }
    
    void Allocator::notifyReturn()
    {
      unsigned state;
      do {
        state = notify;
        if (!(state & Waiting) || (state & Posted)) return;
      } while (notify.cmpXch(state | Posted, state) != state);
      // Claim the stop obligation before touching Stack. An empty/drained provider
      // can outlive Stack and must not read its pointer on ordinary final returns.
      stack->returnedTx(this);
    }
    
    void Allocator::wait(Zi::IOBufWait &request)
    {
      if (stack) stack->waitTx(this, request);
      else IOBufPool::wait(request);
    }
    
    void Allocator::cancel(Zi::IOBufWait &request)
    {
      if (stack) stack->cancelTx(this, request);
    }

## Assistant

`slot(packet)` returns a stable pool-local buffer index, including when `packet` points inside the buffer.

Its production users are:

- **Zutcp receive accounting:** [`retainRx()`](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpMx.cc:1202) uses the index to charge a retained physical buffer to a connection’s `RxAccount`. Aliases of the same buffer are charged once.
- **Zutcp buffer return:** [`Allocator::free()`](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpAlloc.cc:107) publishes that index to an Rx-owner return list before freeing the backing. Rx later removes the retained-frame charge.
- **AF_XDP internals:** send, completion, receive and teardown use slot indices to address preallocated bookkeeping directly.

It was added to **`Zi::IOBufPool` in commit `3892a86f`**, when the refactor replaced concrete `Zxdp::BufPool` access with the generic pool interface. `slot()` already existed on the concrete pool; promoting it preserved those existing callers.

So its public-interface purpose is specifically **Zutcp’s physical receive-buffer accounting**. Generic Zi allocation does not itself require it, apart from the default `owns()` implementation. It exposes backend buffer identity across the abstraction boundary; that is the design dependency to assess.

## Assistant

The current implementation uses it to **prevent retained packets from exhausting the shared Rx pool**.

Zutcp can retain received backing for out-of-order data or application-held slices. If all buffers remain held, the backend cannot replenish receive descriptors—even for ACKs or other packets needed to make progress.

It therefore tracks:

- A global retained-buffer limit.
- A per-connection limit.
- A reserve left available for receiving more packets.

When a limit is reached, [the receive path](/home/count0/src/z/zutcp/src/ZutcpConnection.hh:3800) refuses additional out-of-order retention; contiguous data can instead be copied into heap backing so the physical buffer returns to the pool.

Counting bytes alone does not measure this resource: many small packets can occupy many physical buffers.

**This accounting is an admission policy, not the buffer ownership mechanism.** Reference counting already handles lifetime and freeing. `slot()` exists here because this policy uses a preallocated entry per physical receive buffer, avoiding duplicate charges for aliases and tracking final returns. That is why Zutcp currently needs stable buffer identity; receiving TCP itself does not inherently require this particular accounting scheme.

    # Zxdp AF_XDP and DPDK backends
    
    * **Author:** Huw Rogers
    * **Date:** 2026-11-16
    * **Updated:** 2026-11-17

      historical brainstorming reviews completed; this update is source reconciliation,
      not another review or an implementation/test run.
    
    ## Overview
    
    Add DPDK alongside the existing AF_XDP backend using the current polymorphic
    `Zxdp::Instance`. AF_XDP implementation types live in `Zxdp::Xdp`; DPDK types
    will live in `Zxdp::Dpdk`. Extend the existing `Type` selector and tagged
    `Params` union rather than recreating the earlier Backend/If design.
    
    The direct DPDK path is `Zutcp Tx owner → rte_eth_tx_burst() → DPDK/NIC`.
    Software ring/pcap PMDs exercise that same path without a NIC. No intermediate
    DPDK submission ring, EAL Tx worker or extra scheduler sender is required.
    AF_XDP retains its own scheduler sender for kernel Tx processing.
